LADIES' LETTER.

DEAR Maxim. The blouse is one of the few instances in which a real demand on the score of convenience and expediency has triumphed over a merely vague pronouncement of fashion, and in its victory the philosophical observer may see reflected a result of the widespread rush of women into spheres rather than the purely domestic. Few girls nowa- days have time to make their own clothes. The blouse, shapely of cut, pretty as to trimming and accessories, unending in its colours and fashion- ings, looms large in every outfitter's window, and itself has created a new industry in which thou- sands of women are engaged throughout the year. The present week is not an inopportune one for glancing at the remarkable development of this phase of trade.

new tloth hats are as becoming as any in more sophisticated matera's. One of them, in pale grey, has a perfectly flat crown, round which the brim is folded in irregular curves that make a very fascinating frame for the face and hair. Cream colour seems more in favour than any more positive tint for placing under the brim, but we shall see orange, scarlet, metallic tones of green sad blue when the autumn season is a little older. Gold is also much worn on an under the hat, and when the hair is of a warm and ruddy colour the gold lights it up and suits it remarkably well. Gold ribbon is also used for the loops and aigrettes worn with eveniug dress in the hair, and the gold roses have not quite disappeared, having been found too becoming to be laid aside, for no better reason than that they are no longer a novelty. Twisted loops of black velvet are a favourite decor- ation for fair and grey hair. The lines are very slender, and the bows are very wavy and irregular 4^' outline, and all the more picturesque.
'O the new cloths/and serges for winter wear, which are of a beautifully soft texture, light as well as warm, the favourite colours for outdoor wear are a warm tone of nut-brown and a dark

grey, which might be taken for black in a dull light. Both these colours go well with furs, and that is always a consideration in the choice of a winter walking costume. There are many whc are opposed to the everyday wearing of Inc...as hygienically an error. They believe that even the best ventilated fur capes and coats do not equal cloth and velvet in this particular: and they think that the wearing of fur round the neck weakens the throat and renders it susceptible to chill. This is all true enough, as applied to the question of habitually wearing fur ; but in very cold, frosle weather it offers a protection for which most people are truly thankful, and which very few would be found willing to refuse.

shape which is one of the prevailing styles in hats at the present moment is low and soft-crowned in velvet, has a straight, round brim, and sits flatly on the head, not at all in a becoming style. Toques are either raised up in front very much off the face, for which the hair requires to be worn pulled out like an aureole above the forehead or tilted for- ward over the right side of the face, raised up by a chou or flowers on the left side. Most of these toques are merely twists of drap de feutre, in deep cream, old rose, ice-blue, or mauve shades, and are the ideal accompaniments of tailor frocks for morn- ing wear. Many have one corner of the felt left loose to fall in a fan-shaped end on to the hair be- hind, handkerchief fashion. The difficulty with many chapeaux is to decide where the toque ends and where the hat begins, both are so similar in nature.

For the purpose of renovating black and dark woollen dresses liquid ammonia will be found excellent. It not only aets as a solent to the dirt, but serves to revive the colour. About two table- spoonfuls should be added to every gallon of hot water; the woollen fabrics should then be immersed in it and well worked about with the hands, or, still better, with a dolly. They should be folded very smoothly, and passed through a wringer, but on no account wrung with the hands. In preference to this rather hang them over a line (in the air and sun if possible) and allow them to drip ; then, when still very slightly damp, press on the wrong side of the material with a warm (but not hot) iron, and they will look nearly as good as new. Violet, heliotrope, and grey are the only shades that will not bear this process—it will better pay in the end to send them to a cleaner. Black silk may be nicely restored by sponging with equal parts of common malt vinegar to which a few drops of ammonia have been added; no ironing is advisable.
Your loving, Jlortra.

A QUEEIT'. SOLDIER.
By WALTER WOOD, Author of "Barrack and "little&ld," "Famous British Warships," "Through Battle to Pro- motion," "A Captain in the Fusiliers," "A Soldier of the Legion," &c.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Mark Benn, the son of a substantial farmer in Yorkshire, volunteers for service in the Yeomanry, about to be despatched to South Africa. After the farewells due. to • his father and his sweetheart, Lizzie Jackson, he duly embarks, the troop also including his friend Brigg. To his surprise he finds Lizzie Jackson at Capetown as an army nurse, she having left England on a mail steamer,- which had passed the slow-going transport. Benn and Brigg are in a skirmish with three 'Boers. Poor Brigg is shot through the head, but,-nOt before he has wounded one of the Boers, and Benn distinguishes himself by disarming and taking the three prisoners. In a skirmish some days later Benn is twice wounded, and is himself taken prisoner.

div.head: CHAPTER. IX.
div.p: CHAPTER. IX.
TO TIIE CAPITAL.

It was soon made clear to Mark and his companions that they had been cunningly trapped. Of the genuineness of the retreat of .the enemy there was no doubt; they freely confessed that the house had been made too hot to hold them, and that they could not keep the ridges when they remembered the bayonets of the assailants. Frankly they made known that steel at such close quarters was nothing to their liking. But while they had withdrawn readily enough from the top of the kopje, and had hastened over the veld to rejoin their own people, they had not hurried so much as to be blind to the fact that they were being pursued by a body of men who were practically defenceless. This much was seen very soon, but as the field guns and the Maxims chewed unpleasant energy it was considered prudent to lure the Yeomen well away from their supports before turning upon and compelling them to sur- render. The Boers were proud of their achieve- ment, and were in a tolerant and amiable spirit. Amongst them were two or three men who had been educated in England, and jocosely assured their captives that this visit by them to Pretoria would be followed by a return visit to London—a visit of prolonged duration. They were also assured that they would be by no means forlorn in the Transvaal capital, which even then was glutted with British prisoners of war. "They are caught so easily—some of them," sneered one of the captors. "Very likely; they're not so slick at bolting " as some people,. answered Mark, who heard the words. Prisoner though he was, he was undaunted, and recklessly flung back the taunts which had been levelled at his countrymen. The speaker scowled, but did not add to his remarks. Wade, riding at Benn's side, urged him in a loud whisper to keep his tongue still, lest he should do himself and them an evil. "It's the only thing I've got left to fight with," said Mark, bitterly; but all the same, wishful not to jeopardise his comrades' safety, he kept himself in check, and for the present rode on in silence. By this time, he was suffering intensely from his wounds and from thirst. Other men were injurod, but none so seriously as he. For the most part theirs were clean wounds in the flesh, the bullets having passed completely through the tissues. So far as his shoulder went Mark was but little dis- turbed. It was his leg that troubled him, and with respect to this he supposed that the bullet was still in the limb. He said as much to Wade. "Well, if it is so, why should' you trouble so much about being bagged? You'd be no more good for fighting, anyway. You'd have to go under the X-ray machine an' get mauled about pretty considerably by the doctors. You're just •as well here as any- where else." "Can't we ask them to stop a minute so that I can tie a handkerchief round and get a drink I'm nearly dead with thirst." "So are we all, so are they, too, an' the horses as well," answered Wade, whose own appearance shewed how much he'suffered. "But so long as we're in the open here, an' so long as there's a chance of any of our lot coming after us an' trying to do a rescue, there'll be no consideration either for your leg or our throats. Ugh I'd give my immortal soul for a drink of anything that's drinkable." The party hurried on, mile after mile, the captors constantly looking back to see that they were not followed, and ahead and aside to make certain that they were not cut off. But they were safe; the chance of pursuit had passed, and the Major on the summit of the kopje was even yet enduring the agony of seeing some of his men .marched off as prisoners of war. He alternately cursed himself and the subaltern, but very soon assigned all the blame to himself. This he did the more fervently when the junior and the rest of the fallen were brought in by the stretcher-bearers, and when, simnel without a close look, one of the surgeons had shaken his head and murmured that the subaltern would fight no more. The captives had drunk all the water in their bottles before the fighting began, and were now enduring exquisite torture from thirst. Mark raised his bottle to his lips and sucked at it until his mouth seemed to burn; but there was not so much as a drop of moisture left, and he groaned. Already his sufferings were as much as he could bear, but he restrained himself and jogged on through the heat and dust. Perhaps it was because he was feeling somewhat light-headed that his imagination dwelt persistently on that long day in the hayfield at home when he had stopped from time to time to take a long, deep draught of home- brewed ale. Reeling in his saddle, with nerveless hands still clasping the reins, with his bloodshot eyes rolling slowly in their sockets, and his head sinking jerkily from time to time upon his chest, with the dust still mercilessly beating upon his blackened face and into his open mouth, Mark went on in a sort of stupor. From this he was roused by cries of delight. He raised his head and found himself in the midst.of a struggling crowd of men and horses. For a mgment he had thought of rescue, but he found that it was, to him just then, far better luck than that. The body had come across water, and already there were Yeomen lying down and drinking what seemed like rand. Even then Mark gave his horse rein, and let him drink his fill before he thought of himself. Then, forgetful of the wounds and the intense pain they caused him, he got to the ground, bent down, and thick and dlscoloured,though the water was, drank of it with i delight such as he had never known. It seemed as if he could never drink enough. Time after time he drank afresh, and at last, with a sigh of thankfulness and pleasure, he rose to his feet and staggered to his horse's side. He got , a foot into a stirrup and tried to mount, but he failed. He tried again, tried desperately, hatinA the thought of giving in, but still he did not suc6ed. For the third time, mustering all his energyidie tried to swing into his seat as he had swims' when the subaltern gave the order to mount. Trmis' time the effort •overcame him. His privations end wounds got the better of him ; his head seemed to whirl and the ground seemed to spin, and he fell heavily upon the veld. Wade, already in the saddle, saw his attempts, and was riding up to help him. He reached Berm just as he fell over. His ettert to save him from the fall was useless, and he had to dismount before lie could get his comrade into his seat. Other Yeomen gave assistance, and with one on each side of him Mark, unconscious of what was passing, performed the last part of the journey to the Boer head- quarters. When he regained his senses he saw that he was lying on a couch in what he knew to be a farm- house. Instinctively he felt his shoulder and his Leg. Both the wounds had been washed and as be might have treated them Lc: gahe yf bafor des g ed' handkerchief had in each case been that no trained nurse or medical man had been at wrapped round and tied in a knot. It was clear work upon him. Instantly he thought of Lizzie, and longed for her presence. A placid, stout woman of about fifty years was THE MOST NUTRITIOUS. standing arm table near him. He stared at her, but E p psys passing did not notice him, nor for that matter did she pay attention td anything that was psing in the house or near it. ' Her entire thought seemed to be devote to her FiATEFUL—COM FORTING. dough and her task, and it was only when she had C C got the last batch of loaves in the oven that she appeared to know that time prisoner was awake. Mark had heard 'so much of the bloodthirstiness lied cruelty of the people against whom he fought that he was surprised to find that he felt now as he might have felt if he had had an accident in the hunting-field or when rabbit-shooting. He saw but Little difference between this room and the ulacid

I woman, and the living room at Hill To Farm and his own mother. "Well, young man," said the woman, with a quiet smile. "Well, missus," answered Mark, taking it as a matter of course that he should be addressed in his own language. "Who brought me here?" "They did," was the answer.
"When ? " asked Mark. "Yesterday," was the reply. "What!" he exclaimed. 'Do you mean to say that I've been here since then ? "
_ "Yes, they carried you in, put you down, aad left you. I tied the handkerchiefs on. It was all I could do." _

"Thank you," said Mark. "I'm a farmer myself," he added, marvelling as he spoke that he should say this thing. "Are you ? " said the woman. "Then why did you come here? I mean, why did you come out to this country ? " "To fight, answered Mark. "What for? " she demanded. "I don't know," he replied. It was the simple truth. He had not the remotest idea as to the reasons why the war had broken out. His own interest began and ended with his determination to shew that he was a real soldier, and not a, sham.

"I don't, either," said the 'woman. "Suppose any soldiers from another country went to your farm, what would you do?" "Kill 'em, of course," said Mark, energetically. The woman smiled. "That's jnst what were doing," she said. All the stories Mark had heard of Boer atrocities rushed back to his mind. He rose on the couch as lie inquired: "Where are the other chaps ?" The woman laughed. "Come," she said, "I don't mean that. I mean in fight!" "There's fighting and fighting," said Mark, with a bitter remembrance of the death of Brigg and the attempt made on himself. If the woman knew what he meant, she did not say anything. "The other men are out there—you can see them getting ready. They're going on to Pretoria by train. You're going with 'em, if you're well enough. I daresay you will be—you'll get good doctors and good nursing there—at least, they say so. Here comes the Cornet." The door opened, and the man who the day before had taunted Mark came in. He was evidently a man of authority. He addressed Mark roughly, but not unkindly. "Are you fit to come with us ? " he asked. "Yes, if you can shove me into a waggon or a train," answered Mark, not mincing his words. "I can't walk, and I can't ride." "You're a rough customer," said the Field Cornet. _ _ .

"It's rough work—and a rough country," lsnswered Mark. "And rough people, eh ? " said the Field Cornet, quite good-humouredly. "Well, you aren't angels," said Mark. Something in the answer seemed to put the Field Cornet into good spirits. "And we're not devils, either, Mr. Yorkshireman," he said. "Now then, we'll get you into the train over there, and see that you're all right till you get to Pretoria. Some of you have been wanting to see the President—you'll soon be satisfied. They'll come for you in a minute or two." The Field Cornet left the house. . .

"Look here, inissus," said Mark, "you've set me thinking. There's something in what you say. What's your name?" "Boota," said the woman. "What for ? " "Because I want to remember it. If I can an you a good turn, I should like to. Mine's ,Benn —Mark Benn. I'll write my address down, if you'll give me a pencil and some paper." The woman brought him an old envelope and a thick stump of joiner's pencil. "There," said Mark. "That's where I live. Our people have lived there for generations. Have you a husband ? " "Yes," said the woman. "Any sons "One." "Where are they ?" "Both at Pretoria, in a commando there, or doing police work." "Well, if they ever come to England, and want a good turn doing, tell em where I'm to be seen, will you?" "I will," the woman promised. "You've done well by me," said Mark, gratefully. "It's only what I've done by the others," she said. "That makes it all the better," said Mark. "I say, I can't reckon you up. Your name isn't English, but your face is—and you talk good English, too." "I ought to," she answered. "My father was an English soldier. He deserted in the 'forties and married a Boer woman ; and I've often heard him say be was never sorry for what he did, either." "By George !" exclaimed Mark. "This country gets over me! Well, here they come with the stretcher. If I can do you a good turn, I shan't forget." "I'm sure you won't," said the woman. "If you meet my hubsand or son, remember me to 'era, will you 2 " "I will," Mark promised, earnestly. He gazed for several seconds at her, then added in a deep voice : "By George ! missus, I'm sorry for you. If I'd-known, I wouldn't have come out." "That's what I'm thinkin' of ri lot of you," said the woman. "Here, put this cake in your pocket—and take a drink of this coffee." Mark did both.
As they carried him from the house he stretched forth his hand and seized that of the farmer's wife.
"Good-day, missus," he said. "I hope your people will come back all right." "And I hope you'll get home palely, too," she answered.
She watched them put the trooper into the carriage at the station, which was very near the farm; and watched with dim eyes the train which steamed away with its prisoners for the capital,
CHAPTER X.

div.head: NURSE AND IDLER.
div.p: NURSE AND IDLER.

Amongst the idlers rim naa gone to the seat of war from England was the youthful Lady Mildred Maud. The society functions of London had palled on her, and, filled with the longing to do something which should get her talked about by men and women whom she knew, she had packed up numerous boxes, taken with her a sober maid, and sailed from Southampton by a steamer carrying troops and munitions of war. Someone had given her a large and beautiful bouquet, and carrying this she had embarked for the Transvaal. Without any genuine training, moved only by the craze for change and notoriety, she assumed the garb of a nursing sister, and in a whirl of excitement and false enthusiasm, embarked for the Cape. More curious to see what she could do than amxious to assist its . victims, Lady Mildred pushed her way to as near the front as the authorities would let her go. The devastation and danger of the trip dismayed her, and more than once she thought of turning back and going home. But she found that by carefully preserving her role as a mere spectator, keeping out of the way of all hard work and unpleasantness, and with the help of her maid and her many boxes, she could maintain her. health and prettiness. Despite all snubs—and they were many—from clever surgeons and gifted officers, men who knew the value of every soldier's life and every ounce of food and drink and foot of breathing-space and living-room, And resented 'the presence of those who did not tsork, only wasted and consumed, she insisted upon haunting the hospitals and military bases, meddling here and there with some half- formed purpose of doing good and throwing distinction upon .herself.

She was hopelessly useless, a mere butterfly hanger-on, but she refused to see it, and remained • supremely placid and contented with herself. Men died of disease and wounds about her, but through all these horrors her selfishness and care kept her safe; one or two overworked nurses— women who had gone to the front mostly because of their humanity, and because it was in this way that they had been trained to earn a living—died at their posts. • Seeing them succumb, Lady Mildred began to rear for herself, and to wonder whether it would aot be well to return to Capetown and go home before matters grew worse. But her pride and vanity chained her to the town. Pride prevented her from doing what would look like a cowardly act; vanity moved her to stay, for occasionally a newspaper correspondent would allude to Lady Mildred's presence at the front, and a photo- grapher—who was ready to snap at anything from a Fretty nurse to a shrapnel-shattered corpse—would beg to be allowed to take a picture of her in her uniform. The newspaper patagraphs were to her as the breath of life, while it was positive!), exhilarat- ing to think of the sensation which would be created amongst her friends by the appearance of her photograph—perhaps styled "An Aristocratic • Angel of Mery "—in an ifh.astraked jeureal some- where.

' Lady Mildred acted alone. Them were friends of hers who had come out also to see what they Sould and satisfy their curiosity; but from these she kept aloof, wishing that whatever she did should be done by her alone and not shared by anyone. It would detract from the distinction of an adventure to have it shared by a friend, and she recognised that there were likely to be times when it would be much more easy for a single nurse to get from place to place than for a party.

As well as she was able—for there were stern officers who did not believe in the presence at the theatre of war of any unnecessary person, and put every possible obstacle in her way—Lady Mildred got from place to place. This she did largely by influence, because she was the niece of a man high in command in the campaign, and her father was a member of the House of Lords, and one to whom military authorities were wont to lend a listening ear.

Most of the officers frankly gave way before her onslaughts; only one had the courage stoutly to contest her right to be where she was or to proceed. further. Ile was an obscure army surgeon, a practitionet who worked with all the skill and strength that God had given him in the interests of the soldiers whom he loved, because of what they were and what they did. His name was Donald, and he came from a Scotch University where he had paid for the culture of his intellect by ths labour of his hands, working by day as a skilled artisan, so that he might earn his lecture fees and lodging charges. He was as bold in putting into execution his ideas as he was fearless in adopting them, and one of his ideas was that all idlers should be driven away from the front with ruthless impartiality. In particular was he bitter on the subject of men or women who had pushed their way to the fringe of fighting so that they might see all they could and yet themselves take no hurt. Lady Mildred, with her maid and most of her boxes, had cajoled and brow-beaten her way to a base hospital where Donald and Lizzie were employed and to which a large number of wounded men were being brought after a disastrous battle.

7 - Surgeon-Major Donald had himself gone on to the field of fight, and, reckless of shell and bullet, had done what he could to save a limb or life. But he had had to return, and with a heavy heart leave the field littered with the wounded, many of them his countrymen. At nightfall he left the field, knowing that many helpless soldiers were lying there ; but knowing, too, that it would be hard to find them till the day broke, and that meanwhile the hospital was filled with those who needed instant help. It made him dumb with grief to see the ambulance waggons come in, a never-ending stream, with the wounded and dying. lie spoke but rarely, and then mostly to say that this or that case was hopeless. He notics6 specially the work of two women near him. On of them, pale-faced, flurried, overcome with the horrors of the scene, was standing impotently ; the other, a trained nurse, was doing her work with a woman's gentleness and a man's strength. Wounded man after wounded man was washed by her alone, and yet instinctively she knew when a new arrival wanted his intense thirst relieving, and hurried forward with water. Her uniform was untidy and dirty, her eyes were heavy and her face was pale for want, of sleep, but she never faltered in her duty. Unmindful, as it seemed, of all war's horrors she went about her task of helping Donald and his staff.

" The men who were brought in belonged to various arms—cavalry, artillery, infantry, regulars and irregulars, British and Colonials. Here and there was a man whose rank or branch it was almost impossible to tell, so torn and damaged was his clothing. For a long time Lizzie—for the hard-working nurse was she—felt that there was one gleam ot comfort in the gloom of human suffering and misery before her, and that was that there were nc Yeomen amongst the wounded, none, at least, sc far as she could tell, and by this time she was pretty quick in distinguishing the troops. She began to hope wildly that the Yeomen had not taken part in the fight, since she knew that Mark's company was not very far away, and that if Yeorner at all had been engaged he was probably amongst them. But the very last of the men brought in— one unconscious from a shell-wound, the othes suffering from a shattered foot—belonged, she say' at once, to Mark's own company. She hastened to the help of these last two, anxious to learn what had happened, and yet fear- ful of the worst.
The senseless trooper was carried from her view at once ..to the lips of the other she held a cup of water which he drained at a draught, then asked for another.

"Ah!" he said, with a long sigh of pleasure, "that's the best drink I ever tasted. It's bettes than sweltering out there and seeing what's happening to poor chaps worse off than I am. should have gone mad if l'd had to stand it much longer. How many of us have come in here, miss, up to now ? " "I don't know," answered Lizzie. "About six, I should think--I mean six of your lot." "Six!" he exclaimed. "I should have thdught the whole company was here. anyway, it must be pretty well done for. I suppose you've heard of the wretched luck we've had ?" "No," said Lizzie, tremblingly.

'"Lieutenant Slade and about"' score of men were tripped as neat as ninepence. The Lieutenant was killed. I know that, because I saw him buried, and the rest were carried off. We couldn't du - anything, the Boers were so sharp about it. We should have gone after them, but another big lot turned up and let us in for this fight." ,The trooper writhed as he spolce. "Ugh!" he said, grimly. "I suppose it'll soon be iny turn. Good God! But this is worse than the fighting.' "Was—was there a trooper called Benn with you?" she asked, desperately. "Benn—good old Mark Benn," said the wounded man." There was so. He was one that they walked off with. I heard somebody who was watching from the top of the kopje where we were say he was sure that Mark was hit. Hullo, what's the matter? Did you know him ? " "Yes, 1 knew him," said Lizzie, with a white face. "Look here," said the trooper, energetically. "He's all right; hurt or no hurt, he could kee/ his saddle. Of course, he'll see no more of the bother now that they've got him as a prisoner of war. Don't you worry. "Worry about what ?" asked a supercilious voice. "Oh, nothing, a friend of the lady's," answered the trooper, turning his head so that be could see the speaker. "Lady? Which lady? Oh, the nurse," said the owner of the voice. 'Really, my good creature, I'm surprised that you should be talking to one ol the poor fellows like this. My gbod man, what can I do for you ?" It happened that the good man, when at home, was a shrewd young manufacturer, with a heavy bank balance, partner in a firm employing at least two thousand people, somewhat of a god in his cr.' community, and accustomed to be made much VA He was by no means used to hearing himself addressed in the patronising tones of a mistress speaking to a servant, and he looked at the speakes with glowing eyes. He resented, too, the sneer at the nurse beside him.

"Thanks," he said, finding his tongue at last. "I shall be quite satisfied if you let me alone." The fussy new arrival looked amazed, then intensely annoyed. She had never before been addressed like that by anyone. It seemed impossi• ble that she could have been understood, and, unwisely, she said as much to Lizzie, making it clear from her demeanour that to speak at all to her was an act of some condescension.

"I'm afraid the man is delirious," she said, "You'd better have him looked to at once. POO! thing !",,There *as more contempt than pity in thc last of her sentences. "Come, she added, "did you hear me ? " _

Lizzie turned to the wounded man and got him ready for the surgeon's attentions. She paid no heed whatever to the speaker. " Really, " exclaimed Lady Mildred, "this insolence is intolerable. You cannot understand who I am. I &kali certainly report your behaviour to the doctor."

"I shall be ,mite ready to explain it to him," answered Lizzie: quietly. "Now I must leave you and see to those poor creatures over there," she *aid, speaking to the trooper. 14 gave her a grateful look and managea ee. i.vhisper : is she when she's at home ? " "A woman of title," answered Lizzie.

_ "Ah I thought, as much," said the:trooper. "Come out for a bit of sport, eh? Well, thank God, she's the first of her sort I've seen, and I hope she'll be the last. If she bothers me again I shall be rude." Lady Mildred did report the matter of the nurse to the doctor, and did it so indiscreetly and at such an inopportune moment that Donald entirely lost his teinper, and, is he expressed' Ulster, let himself go without putting much brake on. In five minutes he had explained his views on the subject of. nursing generally, and fashionable nurses in particular, and had made it palpably impossible that the same roof \ could shelter himself and the lady for one hour ihger than was needful.

When the pressure of his work was over and ha had time to reflect, he was mindful of his error in making an enemy of a woman who had so much in her power; but the surgeon was stubborn, and refused to yield in any way or to deviate from the atand that he had taken. When he understood that his presence was required at another hospital nearer to the front and that Lizzie would accompany him, he perceived without much difficulty that influence had been at work, that the. little fight had been fought, and that Lady Mildred had won.

"That's one advantage," he said, bitterly, "of being able to get a listening ear. If I used all my wit and all my power for the rest of my life to get the same attention I couldn't do it. Well, my girl, I've lived down worse things. I shall soon get over this. I don't mind going nearer to the front. I suppose you don't, either?" "I'd a thousand times rather be there than here," answered Lizzie ; but she did not explain that the reason for this preference was that the nearer to the capital she got the nearer she would be to Mark, (To coatinuect

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAI.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAI.

Despite Queen Alexandra's express desire that only home-made fabrics should be wore by those women bidden to the coronation ceremony,it seems highly prob- able, judging by the orders which have been received abroad, that foreign-made materials will predominate on this all-important occasion. It has been frequently said that it is the great middle-class of women which errs most in preferring foreign goods, or 13 indifferent on the point altogether, and that middle-class shop- keepers frequenas fad it necessary to bestow a foreign name upon home manufactures, in order to render them more attractive to their customers. But however. this may be, it would appear that the upper class of women are not without reproach in this particular matter. And, one and all, we have no excuse for cur lack of patriotism. If our beautiful home-made fabrics are possible for members of cur Royal Family, add for such great ladies as the Duchess of Sutherland, the Marchioness of Londonderry, and the Countess of War- wick, then surely they are possible for all. The Duchess of Cornwall as is well-known, had her entire outfit for her long tour made of British and Irish silks and satins exclusively, and the other materials as far as poaaible were also of home manufacture. Again her Royal Highness is, and always has been, most particular that her children should wear none but hems made fabrics, If we women of these Islands would but follow such an example it would mean prosperity and happiness for many thousands of our countrymen and countrywomen, and personally, we should be gainers ia the end. The children of the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall have grown a good deal during the past seven or eight months, and the difference in their appearance was one of the first'aud most agreeable impressions which greeted their Royal Highnesses on their return home. Prince Edward is in his eighth year, and his brothers and sister are of an age in:which a few mouths makes a striking advance in their growth. The boys look bonny in their simple sailor suits which they generally wear. The Duchess prefers that her children should always he dressed quietly, and even little Princess Victoria Alex- andra, woo is in her fifth year, is invariably most plainly frocked.6lll • - Wien Brilliant weather of almost summer-like warmth and brightness favoured the wedding of Mr. Herbert Glad- stone and Miss Dorothy Mary Paget. The marriage took place at St. Andrew's Church, where the bride- groom's father used frequently to attend, and among the officiating clergy were the Rev Stephen E Gladstorie,Dr. Wickham, and the Rev Harry Drew. Miss Dorothy Drew,the favorite of her grandfather,the late Mr W. E. Gladstone, was one of the three child bridesmaids, the others being Miss Mary Lyttelton and Miss Clarissa Tennant. The presents, which included a silver ink- stand from his Majesty the King, numbered over 600, and the list speaks volumes for the popularity of Mr. Herbert Gladstone amongst politicians of all shades of opinion. 'There were nearly a dozen silver instauds, but duplicates were inevitable in such an unually large number of presents, The remarkable longevity of the Quakers, which has been referred to frequently in the press, has been illus- trated once again by the ease of Mrs Elizabeth Banbury, who died at the age of 108. She was born while France was in the throes of the French Revolution. and was al girl of 13 when William Pitt, and Charles James Fox, passed beyond the strife of parties. Until three years ago we are told Mrs Hanbury--who had been a widow ' since 1869—rose and dressed and spent a portion of each day in light handiwork. We frequently hear of people living to over a hundred, but it is not often that such tales are substantiated by authentic records, as in the case of the late Mrs Banbury and that also of the present Dowager Lady Carew, who recently completed her leetti year. This lady, who was a Miss Cliffe, was married as tar back as 1816. when a girl of twenty, and has been a widow since 1856. Lady Carew has lived under five Sovereigns, and she was able until lately to play whist, and chess. though for the past ' four ur five years she bas rot left her room, and has lately been rather seriously ill. The Ladies' Kennel Association will hold a great show of pets at Earl's Court, on the 20th of this month. The Queen Consort has been a frequent exhibitor at these annual shows, which are most exclusive, and where the most aristocratic dogs may be seen showing off their airs and graces. This year an exception is to be made in allowing more men to enter their dogs. There are bowever, in Society circles, probably more dog fanciers among women than arroag men, whilst the National Cat Club, which has just held its twelfth annual show is entirely supported by women, and has amongst its patrons Princess Victoria of Schleswig Holstein, the Duchess of Bedford, the Countess of Warwick, and the Countess of Aberdeen. Mr S L Bens US3II has reprinted from a magazine his article on the cruelties which are practised in training performing animals. Whether or not his statements are in all cases exact,there is at any ratP,no room for doubt that performing animals are in many instances sub- jected to great cruelty. Even the monkeys which are carried round the streets by Italian boys and which are taught balancing on a tight rope, skipping, sparring with boxing gloves, and making-believe to be dead, are not treated kindly, as anybody may perceive lay, close observation, and the public would do well to discourage all such exhibitions. Ts cut sprays, groups, or simple leaves from glace silk, ontline and vein them with fine jet, and mount them on lace, chiffon, or ci 6pe, is work that can be very' easily accomplished, and at little cost, during the long winter evenings that be before us. A most de- lightful blouse can be built of such fabric, care being of course necessary that the tones in evidence in the sprays ' etc, and the foundation, match or blend with the skirt with which they are to be worn. For less dressy work, cretonne can take the place of glace silk, the sprays, groups, flowers, or leaves, detached therefrom being secured to the foundation by means of button- holing with shaded embroidery silk, In strips this form of trimming is most effective for a morning blouse. Skirts show no sign of growing any fuller above the knees, indeed, if such a thing were possible, they se. m to be more clinging there than ever. Pockets therefore are an impossibility, unless One has them placed in a flounce, but even here they almost invariably give some evidence of their pretence. The majority of women depend upon the petticoat pocket, lint this too ta; its disadvantage in being difficult of access ; others cling Ito the bags, or satchel. In bags, the bead variety is the most popular. When in colours, the beads should match the gown of course, but these come rather costly, and the steel bead bag beside looking well, has the dis- tinct advantage of going with any toilette one may possess. To be gracelul, these bags should be SUE- ' pended by chains. or by ribbons of sufficient length to allow them to fall well below the knees. The" storm " variety of collar would seem to be 11 almost extinct. It is said that furriers plotted its downfall, in order to enconrage the wearing of the boa, but to whomsoever we owe the change it is welcome indeed. The intense eusceptitility to chill induced by the very high collar was productive of much illness, and the exclusion of air about the neck while vigorous exercise was in progre.s,was highly unhygienic. Gener- ally speaking we muffle ourselves much less than for- merly, a hapry state of affairs brought about undoubt- edly by the athletic, open air lives we have led of late l years. MADGE.

div.head: Pollution of the Ship Canal.
div.p: The Pollution of the Ship Canal.

At a meeting of the Mersey and Irwell Joint Committee in Manchester on Monday, it was de- cided to take proceedings against the Salford Cor- poration for continued pollution of the lrwell. Mr V K Armitage said the committee had been patient to the extent of weakness with the Corporation. Mr Alderman Mellor, of Ecclee, described the con- dition of the Ship Canal as having been more vile and filthy during the last summer than it had been since it was opened. The case of Manchester was also considered. It was stated that Manchester bad been endeavouring to meet the wishes of the committee, and the consideration of the case of he city was adjourned for six months.

BroncLitis is the most fatal disease in Ecgland next to cnrsumption ; then heart disease. pneumonia, and scar- latina. At Oxford nn Tuesday Frederick Walters, newsagent' was fined £5 and costs for employing a boy under eleven to sell cewspapers in the streets. div.p: 3 REAKFAST-$U PREF',
AGAINST PRACTICAL JOKING. Children May be Harmed by a Fright.

There are few towns in which instances cannot be re- called where a child's whole future life has been seriously affected by some silly fright to which it had been subjected, says a Briktol newspaper. Happilylthe consequences are not always lasting, though they may cause great trouble and uneasiness. We were led to these reflections when making inquiries into the circum- stances surrounding a miserable misadventure which befell a little girl named Hannah Smith, thirteen years old, at Bristol.

_ "When we were living down in the valley there,about two years ago," said the child's father, " our next- door neighbour asked my little girl to run an errand for him. She and her elder sister went ;.together, and as they were coming back a man ran after them and frightened them. The older girl was not affected very much, but Hannah was dreadfully scared and upset,and when she got borne she was all of a shake and quite hysterical. She continued in this condition for 60020 time, gradually growing worse. She could not keep still. Her eyes and limbs twitched continuously and she was shaking all over." She was so bad," put in Mrs Smith, " that I had a good cry over the child many a time. Her nerves seemed completely upset. She crew s.a weak and too, that it was pitiful to see her. her appetite left bee and she was so low-spirited that she often burst out crying. Her rest was broken and she used to scream. cut in her sleep. We took her to a doctor, and he said she had a bad attack of St Vitus' dance. MAGISTRATES AND ,THE NEW POLICE .COURT. "A Public Scandal." ' The heating apparatus at the new Warrington Police Court is not yet in working order, and on Monday this called forth a strong complaint from the magistrates. Before the businiss was proceeded with, Mr F. Monks (the presiding magistrate) said he bad been asked by the Bench to say that it was nothing Is than a public scandal that magistrates should be brought there weak after week, day after day, to sit in a room that waa cold. Some magistrates last Friday complained of the cold being very bitter. Ha thought it was nothing less than a public scandal that the magistrates and the pub- lics should be brought there to sit in a cold room like that. He hoped tbe authorities would take notice of Ude fomplaint. So far as he was concerned, he should not come again until the rosin was warmed, and he was authorkzed by the Bench( present that morning to say they were very much of the same feeling. Except for the great Inconvenience to the public they should have adjourned the cases until the place bad been warmed. bur to prevent that inconvenience they were prepared to go through their duties that morning, under very unpleasant and uncomfortable circumstances. The business was then proceeded with, and durinr the hearing of a case the Chairman asked Mr Steel (who was defending some lads charged with footballing in the streets) to be as brief as possible as he did not wish to stay in the building longer than was necessary. Mr Steel said he quite agreed with the Chairman's reniargr. He was present at the Court last Friday and he was then suffering from a cold. He was very much worse that morning and it was all through sitting in that cold place. The acoustic properties of the Court are by no means perfect,and instead of being placed in the dcck the prisoners were allowed to stand immediately in front of the magistrates' clerk's desk in order that the Bench Imight hear what they had to say.

div.head: "AT HOME" AT THE TOWN HALL
div.p: "AT HOME" AT THE TOWN HALL

A pleasant function took place at the V. ,arington Town Hall on Monday evening, when the members of the Workingmen' s Infirmary Committee and their wives and friends and the nurses of the Warrington District Nursing Association were invited to an " At Some" given by the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs Roberts). Toe nurses were unable to take advantage of the hopitality extended by Alderman and Mrs Roberts, but the members of the Committee and their wives and friends were present in good mom- beer. Amongst those present were t—Miss Roberts, Mr Gordon Roberts, Mr and Mrs J I. Tunstall,Mr Charles and Miss White, Mr Frank and Miss Milling, Ceuncillor John Roberts (chairman of the Workingmen' 4 Com- mittee), and Mr D Fanshaw (deputy -hairman). The Council Chamber had been tastefully decorated for the occasion, plants having been tastefully arranged by Mr Parker, bead gardener. The reception was from seven to eight in the Councillor Chamber, during which time Mr Plrcy Randall's band efficiently played the following selection of music r—March, " Brazilian ''; overture, Mignettnn ; pizzicato gavotte. "Sylvia ' ; selection, " Patience" ; waltz, " Brise des Nuits," and one or two other pieces. A concert was given by the following artistee, all acquitting themselves very creditably r Quartetto. "Nellie Grey," Orpheus Glee Party ; song, " A Life's Story," Miss Arline Harrison ; quartette, " Simple Simon," Glee Party (encnred) ; song, " 0 Promise Me," Mies Arline Harrison (encored) ; qu,rtette, Orpheus Glee Party. Dancing was commeneed at nine and was continued with zest until eleven o'clock. the music being supplied by Mr Randall'A band. Light refreshments were served, the catering of Mr and Mrs 'Fowls giving complete satisfaction. Counnillor JOHN ROBRIRTR, in proposing a vote oF thanks to the Mayor and Mayoress alluded to the work of the Workingmen's Committee since the year 1880. At chat time there were, he explained. only about ten or fifteen numbers ; now there were 120. They had had some hard work to do to bring shout such a desir- able state of things, and much credit was due to the members for their efforts. It was very kind of the Mayor to appreciate the work of the committee, and to show his appreciation in such a public manner. It was bati s- factory to know that the tunds of the committee had increased steadily, and last year they were able to hand over to the Infirmary no less a sum than £l,OOO, which was clear proof that the committee were doing their duty ; and he was sure they were prepared to continue their good work. They hoped to be able to hand over from £l,OOO to £1,200 ner annum. (Applause.) Mr. FANSHAW seconded, and said the fact that his Worship had acknowledged the services of the commit- tee would induce them to throw more determination than ever into their work in aid of the Infirmary. They only hoped that the invitation extended to them that evening by the Mayor would be extended to them by subsequent mayors, (Applause). The motion was then carried with acclamation. The MAYOR Paid it afforded him perhaps more pleasure to see the guests than it afforded them ti be present. He felt that the Workingmen's Committee was a great power for good so far as that noble institution the In- -firmary was concerned. As Mr. Fanshavr had remarked they were there to spend a pleasant evening, arid he hoped they would make themselves perfectly at home and use the rooms which had been thrown open for their reception. On behalf of the Maynrese and himself he thanked his friends for their very kind vote of thanks. (Applause.)

ILLNESS OF THE BUDWORTH MEDICAL OFFICER, Dr. Bower, medical officer for the Budworth district, wrote informing the Bard that during the past three weeks through illness he had been incapacitated from work, and he asked that he might be granted a week's leave of absence. to recruit his health His district during his illness had been attended to by his deputy and Dr ofi Steven who resided at his house, and would d during his absence "GUY FAWKES DAY." The Master repor.ed that Mr. Parkinson, Bridge- street, Warrington, bad given a parcel of fireworks for the use of the children to commemorate Guy Fawkes

day. A vote of thanks was accorded the donor. PERAMBULATORS FOR THE BABIES. The Chairman asked what had been done respecting the perambulators that were to be purchased. Mr Norman replied that the committee were still con- sidering the question. They were making full inquiries BO that they would get them at the cheapest rates. The Chairman of the District Committee,Mr reported that there were 153 inmates at present in the house. This concluded the business.

Farm Fire at Croft. About eight o'clock the other morning, a fire was qiscovered to have bioken out on the farm occupiedl by Mr John Speakman, Lady-lane Croft. Smoke Was seen issuing from a stack of hay in the yard, and immediately after the flames shot forth. An alarm was raised, 9nd by the kindness of Mrs —""eY. of Heath Farm, communication by tele- P, ."'ne was made to the Leigh Farm Station and in !Attie more than half an hour the brigade arrived with their powerful new steam engine " Victoria" Zortunately there was a good supply of water, but by this time the fire had obtained a firm hold, and as the wind was blowing direct OD to the farm buildings, the firemen directed their attention to atop its progress in that quarter, in 'which they were quite successful, and after a stay of about four hours the brigade were able to leave. Two stacks of hay were destroyed and the loss is esti- mated at about £lOO which is coved by insurance. The origin of the fire is at present unknown. Much sympathy is expressed in the district for Mr and Mrs Speakman who were both under medical treat- ment at the time of the outbreak.

A despatch from Hurley (Wisconsin) [announces that a small theatre there was burned down on Tuesday night. The sleeping apartments of the company were at the top of the building, and nine men and women who were in bed at the time of the outbreak lost their dyes, whilst three other women and one man were eeri- ly injured by burn. been beguiled into holding a baby, it is the look on the face of the baby's mother, eagerly watching . .
him while he does it:

Mrs GUSHINGTON : "And so you were born in the country? How you must have enjoyed the game of hiding in the barn when you were a boy." Mr. Pharmerson : "Well, no, I cannot say I en- joyed it very much. You see my father did the hiding, and all I did was to jump and yell." GUARD: "First, mum?" Lady: "01 course. Guard. I want you to see this child and luggage out safe at Derby; there will be friends to meet her." Guard "Very well, mum, where's her ticket ?" Lady (indignantly): " Ticket ? She's

undo three.' "I WANT my rights 1" fiercely shouted the bass-voiced woman from the platform at the women suffrage meeting. "You can have 'em," piped her husband's timid voice from a far-away corner. "Here's the twins, and I'll go to the neighbours . .

and gather up the other six." LITTLE BROTHER: "Can't you walk straight, Mr. Mangle ? " Mr. Mangle: "Of course I can. Why do you ask ? " Little brother: "Oh, nothin' ; only I heard sister say she'd make you walk straight when she married you. And ma said she'd help her." "How did the cough mixture work that I gave you?" "Badly. I spilled it all over the bed- clothes." "How did you come to do that?" "I didn't notice that they were hanging out on the line in the yard." BLINKERS: "Hello, Winkers. I hear you married a woman with an independent fortune." Winkers (sadly): " No-o ; I married a fortune with an independent woman." JENNIE : " Herbie, it says in this paper that 'another octogenarian's dead. What's an octo- genarian." Herbie "Well, I don't just know what they are but they must be awfully sickly creatures. You never hear o' em but they're dying." A CANDIDATE for municipal favour in a northern municipality had painted the town red—with his bills. Every street hoarding implored the populace to "Vote for Mr. John Brown." " Don't you think the Mr.' a bit out of place?" asked a friend of the candidate. "Well, perhaps so," was the reply; "but you know I can't stand that esquire business." "I CAUGHT myself just in time this morning," exclaimed Mr. Meekton. "I came very near annoying Henrietta quite severely !" "By some remark ? " "No. I startled to whistle " The Girl I left Behind Me," but I stopped before she could recognise it." "She dislikes the tune then ? " "I don't know that she dislikes the tune. But I am sure Henrietta would resent any insinuation that the girl was not taking the lead no matter what the occasion might be." Tins gentleman," said the phrenologist at the open-air performance, "is a close observer—a very close observer." The gentleman on the stand as- sumed a knowing and profound expression of countenance. "So close," continued the phreno- logist, "that I have doubted exceedingly if he would have been here to-night had we charged any ad- mission fee." "Iv you were going to propose to a girl," she said, as the conversation lagged somewhat," "how would you go about it?" "I haven't given the matter much thought," he replied; "but I am inclined to think that I would get down on one knee, like this." "Yes." "And then I would take her hand, like this." "Yes." "And then I would say, " Darling, will you be mine?" "Oh, George !" she exclaimed, this is so sudden, but —but—yes' I will." And all the way home that evening lie kept wondering how it happened, and whether he was quite as smart as he sometimes thought he was. A YOUNG wife came to her mother-in-law heart- broken. "Why, what is the matter, has any- thing happened to Will?" "Oh, mother! He's taken to staying out at night I" wailed the un- happy young woman. "How long has this been goinQ on, my dear? It doesn't seem possible I (lied' to know all about my boy's habits and he never went anywhere he shouldn't. How late does he stay away ? " "You know he usually leaves the office at five o'cleck, mother. The night before last he never got home until seven, and last night he didn't set foot in the house until twenty minutes after eight. Oh, what shall I do ? " A SCHOOL TEACHER sent a little girl home, "with the order to have her mother wash her until she was clean." The child returned shortly afterwards, accompanied by its enraged mother, who said some things not really polite to the teacher, fiuishing with: "She is washed now, how- ever." The only visible evidence of a bath was clean spot around the little one's mouth and nose. The teacher told the mother that she had meant that the child should be thoroughly bathed. She should be put into a tub and washed," she explained. " What ! in a tub?" the woman ex- chimed. "Why, that would kill her ! And, be sie. she's sewed up for the winter." (JAUGIIT.—A num.ber of guests were congregated in toe sinolring.room of a hotel one evening. The conversation turned on the question of physical exercise and endurance. Several of those present gave exaE,rgeratd stories of what they had done and e mid do at one time. " Why, I remember three years ago," said one young man, "I was staying in a house near the Thames. I got up at five every morning, walked ten miles, took off my clothes, and plunged into the river and swam across it three tunes," There was a minute's silence. "Three ii:ftes did ye say, sir?" asked an old Scotchman, who had hitherto kept silence. " Yes, sie ; three times every morning," repeated the boaster. Well, then I'm thinking ye'd find your eines on the wrang side. A MoDEST REQUE3T. " Will you be kind enough to hold this ram for me while I open the gate? It is fastened on the inside, and I must climb over." This remark was made by a man who was standing at a gate on a lonely road, and it was addressed to a stalwart sailor who had just come up. The only other object visible on the long, straight road was the large ram, whose massive crooked horns were being held by the man as the two stood quite still in front of the gate. " Why, sartinly, shipmate," said the obliging tar, as he seiz3d the big horns and relieved the first holder. The latter climbed quickly over the gate. " I thank you very much," he said politely, when he gob to the other side. " You will be surprised to hear that I never saw that ram laefore to-day. The brute attacked t/le about half an hour ago, and wo have been tussling together ever since. As long as you stand before him holding his horns firmly he can't hurt you much. Good-bye. I hope you will be as lucky in getting away from him us I have been." It is not known what the sailor said.

div.head: SWORDS OF HONOUR.
div.p: SWORDS OF HONOUR.
Presentation to Local Officers.

--- There was an interesting ceremony in the Town Hall, Warrington on Saturday afternoon, when the Mayor presented swords of bonour to Captain Applettn, Captain Crosfield and Captain Cary, sub- scribed for by the townspeople, in recognition of their action in serving in the war in South Africe. On the tail of the hilt of each sword is the arms of the borough richly enamelled in relief on a solid silver artistic shield heavily gilt. On the body of the hilt is the crest and motto of the South Lanca- shire Regiment in solid silver ; while the personal crest of the recipient is beautifully enamelled in correct colours, also in relief, on an ornamental solid silver panel. The inscription is etched on the blade in most artistic style and reads as follows on the sword presented to Captain Apple- ton ;—" Presented to Captain F M Appleton by his fellow townsmen, in grateful acknowledgment of his valour and patriotism in volunteering for and serving his country in the war in South Africa, 1901. B. Roberts, Mayor." On the second sword is the name of Captain Cro3field and on the other one that of Captain C F Cary. These swords have been made for Messrs Eustance and Co, who designed and carried out the scheme of decoration which transformed them into swords of honour. There wee a representative attendance in the Council Chamber when the presentations were made. The Mayor was accompanied by the Town Clerk (Mr J Lyon Whittle), and there were also present Colonel Ridgway and Major Ford, Captains Appleton, Crosfie'd and Cary, Quarter-master Potter, Rev W Bracecamp. Alderman Hutchinscn, Councillors Bennett, John Evans. Peacock, Davies emethurst and John Roberts, and Me=srs F Monks, J W 'Hayward. J Herrison,W Furness and G Archer. Several ladies were also present. The MAYOR said that what was almost the last act of his official capacity was one which afforded him very great pleasure to perform and one which he knew would give very great satisfaction to the people of Warrington because of the interest they bad shown in the subject which had once more broucht them together. He had already on behalf of the subscribers and townspeople had the pleasure of presenting formally two presentation swords to Captain Appleton and Captain Crosfield, but they were not quite completed at the time the presenta- tion was made, inasmuch as they had not upon them the Borough Arms, the Arms of the Battalion private crests of the individuals to whom they were presented and the inscriptions. All that eal since been done and their business that morning had an additional interest attached to it because they had also with them Captain Cary, who they would remember was the third officer who volunteered and went out with a section after Vie first detachment. llear, hear.) He was glad in- deed that Captain Cary had come back to them safe and oand. (Applause.) He was very glad to be able to say to him what he said with very great satisfaction to Captain Appleton and Captain Crosfield, that he had laid them under a consider- able obligation by volunteering at the time he did and showing the sense of duty he and those who were associated with him did so markedly in con- nection with a most important period in the his- tory of our empire. (Applause.) Hs sincerely hoped the three gentlemen concerned in this cere- mony would live for many, many years to be re- minded by this little presentation of the good feel- ing which existed between the townspeople and themselves personally, and also of the very warm admiration which all felt of the manner in which they'stood out when the Empire required her eons to do their duty. (Applause.) The Mayor then read the inscription on one of the swords. peaking to Captain Appleton he asked his acceptance of the sword, and again expressed to him on behalf of those he represented Hier high appreciation of his conduct. (Applause.) In pre- senting the second sword to Captain Crosfield he said that what he had said of Captain Appleton ap- plied with equal force to himself, and the pleasure he had had in making the presentation to Captain Appleton was equalled by the pleasure it gave him on behalf of the people ot Warrington to present the sword to him (Captain Crosfisld,) (Applause )1 Turning to Captain Cary he said thin although he was not a Warringtonian by birth, they felt toward him just as cordially as they felt towards their own townsmen in the matter. (Hear, hear.) He had by the fact that he was not associated with them by the same ties perhaps rendered them an even greater obligation by his patriotism in associating himself with their battalion in this matter- (Hear, heat) It afforded him very great pleasure not only to see ' him there and lookieg se well but to make him this presentation on behalf of the town. (Applause.) He was also pleased to present to him a memorial card which he hoped would find a place in his library as long as he lived- (Applause.) Captain APPLTON said he did nct know that he could add anything to the simple words of thanks which he, in conjunction with Captain Crosfield ' addressed to them when the first presentation was made. Now that he had this beautiful sword before him be could emphasize those words of thanks very strongly. His pleasure was the greater because he knew that in honouring them their intention was to honour the men whom he had the honour to command. (Hear, hear.) It was also an additional honour to receive this sword from the Mayor who had shown so much kindness and consideration towards them while they were at the front. (Hear, bear), The sword would be prized by him as his most valued possession, and handed down be hoped to those who came after him. (Applause). Captain CROSFIRLD said be thanked them very much indeed for the sword which he should value very highly. He need not tell them of the very great regret he felt at not being able to go out with the battalion. He was very keen to do so, and it was only because he did not think there was a chance of going out after the first company that he went with the Yeomanry. It was very good of them to give him the sword seeing that he did not go out with Warrington men, and he should value it extremely, and additionally for having teceived it from the hands of the Mayor. (Applause ) Captain CARY said be thanked him very much for the beautiful sword presented to him. He did not think he had deserved the honour of receiving it as he regarded it a sufficient honour to have 'served her late beloved Majesty and the present Kings a veltinteer in South Africa. He woull I value this sword only second to the medal be had {received from the King, and he hoped when he had passed away the sword would remain in his family a; a token that the service which he and his men rendered was appreciated by the towns- people. (Applause.) Colonel RIDGWAY remarked that he .could not let this occasion pass without sayieg a few words, He was very much obliged to them for the hand- some presents made to three of his officers. It really was a very great credit to the battalion that three of:the officers had gained by doing their duty and showing their willingness to fight for their King. such handsome presents. (Hear, hear.) The Volunteers and the Corporation had always been on very good terms. The Corporation had always shown every consideration towards them, and he could add that during the two years' office of the Warrington Field Club. Completely Cured by Bile Beans.

The marvellous manner in which Chas. Forde'a Bile Beans for Biliousness saved a Bolron millworker's life has lately caused considerable comment in Lancashire. Ten year-, ago rheumatic fever left Mrs. Elizabeth Hodg- son, of 13, Boundary-‘treet, Flalliwell, Bolton with hear'-weakness and general debility ; and nothing was able to cure her until she took a course of Clamp. Forde's Bile Bans for Biliousness. In fact, more than once she was believed to bo at death's door. To a " Bolton Journal " reporter who investigated the case, Mrs. Hodgson said :—" I have worked as a weaver in Bolton mills since I was thirteen. Ten years ago while ou a visit to Carlisle—my native place—l had an llwtul attack of rheumatic fever, and for a long time I was so weak that I could not lilt a teaspoon to my mouth. I bad to be fed, and the doctu• wrapped wad- ding all over my body. The fever left me with shot.' - ness of breath, heart-weaknesa, my legs and hands were vPry much swollen, and I could not put my feet to the ground. Later on I was removed to Carlis!e Infirmary and nobody expected me to come out alive. As many as seven doctors visited me one day, and some said I had heart disease. Some time afterwards I asked if I could leave, and I V 748 told I might as well,as I should never be any better. My relatives and friends gave me up ! At the end of seven weeks I was taken out of the Infirmary, and went to Cote Hill, near Carlisle, but even after that I was very ill* I came back ti Bolton, and last August I got a little better and tried to do a bit of work at Messrs Tristram's mill. It was no use however, as became so ill that two weavers had to take me home.

BAND OF HOPE MEETING —The second public meeting of toe Session in connection with the Hill Cliff e and Stockton Heath United Band of Hope was held in Ebenezer Chapel on Monday evening. The Rev. J. S. Hughes presided, and there was a good attendance. The speaker of the evening was Mr. E. J. Nickisson, of Man- chester, who is the deputatiooal lecturer appointed by the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Elope Union, in connection with the,, Million Pennies " scheme, and this lecture was given as a reward to the above society, for their successful efforte in collecting a large number Of pennies towards that scheme, two of its members havmg received medals for collecting large sum'. To encourage the members to take 4 deeper interest in the event, the local committee offered prizes for the best essay written upon the lecture, which was specially illustrated by diagrams, the sut- ject be ing " Alcohol, and the Worker." Mr. Nickisson handled his subject in an instructive manner. There was every appearance that the object of the corn- mitts would be attained. A short programme was gone through, consistirg of recitations by the Misses Eclitn Cole and Annie Broadhurst ; and Masters Herbert Nicholls, Joseph and G Arthur Whitfield; and a dialogue by Misses S E WbitfielJ. L Hall, J Ellison, L Berry, E Coles and Esther Mess. Master G Arthur Whitfield also contributed a selection on the auto-harp, which was much appreciated, Selections on the mandoline.by Miss Wright, of Warringten, were deservedly encored. Miss Clara lienwerthy sang "Was it a dream," in good style, and wee well received. Toe Band of Hope choir,under the care of Mr A H Dunn. rendered two pieces in a praiseworthy manner. Oe the proposition of Mr Sher- bierne,secended by Mr Brereton, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer and artisces,and the singing of the Doxology brought a most successful meeting to a dose. _

NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS. i
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

Many such games as that played at Warrington on Saturday would frighten the spectators away, but, fortunately, it is improbable that there will be another exhibition of the kind this season. Though opposed to the weakest club in the Northern League, Warrington only won by 7 points to 2 points, and then they were somewhat lucky.

It is a fault of Warrington's when opposed to a team with a poor reputation to treat them with scant re• spect and consequently play a long way below form. They started on Saturday as if they had only just to go on the field and look at Brighouse Rangers to win, but they made a sad mistake. At threequarter time the I scores were level, and it was with a sigh of relief that I the home crowd saw Fell se -)re a capital try from a touch•kick by Fish. Previously Warrington had had many chances and tried to take then but something went wrong every time, the bungling by the backs being atrocious. Passing movements frequently took the ball to the line, but the final transfer was always either faulty or not given at aIL IVarrington certainly gave their worst display this:season.
Before the match the players were photographed, an operation which may perhaps have accounted for the poor class of football shown afterwards.

The Brighouse men proved themselvesto be no fools at the elementary methods of the Rugby game. They could push, run, catch and punt as well as most clubs, but combination was sadly wanting,and it is here where they are losing. matches. They have good material in the team and .f the men were only trained to play scientifically the Rangers would not long be at the bottom of the table. Forward they beat Warrington handsomely both in the pack and in the loose, but un- der ordinary circurnst-inces the home backs would have made rings round their less experienced opponents.
I heard after the match that Saville considered the Rangers had played their best game this season. The Brighouse folk do not apparently see much good foot- ball !

The Warrington forwards want a good talking ta. They can play better than they did on Saturday, and they had not the same excuse that the backs had. The latter were cut of form for the time Mho., but it was laziness that affected the front rank.' They would neither push nor follow up with any energy at all, and the committee will find themselves at the mercy of shirkers until they place themselves in such a position that the dropping of a forward or two will not spell certain defeat. Assistance is badly wanted. Even at their best and trying hard the Warrington forwards are not strong enough. The introduction of Fell and Edmondson last season had a magnetic effect. A similar infusion of new blood is required now.

What was the matter with the Warrington backs on Saturday only themselves know. The -halves played very poorly ad the threequarters worse, while even Hallam was not reliable. Dickenson—the usually cool and resourceful centre—was, a regular muff and spoiled more than one nice opening for Harris. It was his off- day I suppose. Fish was only moderate, Harris and Isherwood being the solitary two who did themselves justice.

Fred Saville seems to be just as much the mainstay of the Brighouse team as he was for many years the bulwark of the Stockport club. His play in the rear is as sound and effective as ever, and his kicking powers

IT looks as if the sun The Overthrow of has at last broken Tammany Hall. through the dark bank of fog which has so long lain on the horizon of the United States, and that the political dishonesty and municipal corruption which have been at- tended with such dire results to social morality, especially in the chief city of the States, are to be dispelled. The news which comes of the vieto:r3 of the combined forces of municipal and purity over the Tammany Hall rings in the New York election is an omen of good fortune which cannot be over-estimated. Let it be borne in mind that the same forces which have carried the election of Mr SETII Low for the Mayoralty are those which were successful:Ain forcing Mr Roos VELDT upon his opponents as the nominee for the Vice-Presidency, audit will be seen that the sun' cess which has now been declared is no mere snatch victory or temporary Itriurnpli,;but the arrival at ' maturity of a great power which has been. awakened in the minds and consciences of the American people. For a long time they have submitted to the strings being pulled by corrupt politicians iwhonsought and sold public offices they would goods and chattels. The terrible scandals of police administration which _became matter ofnotoriety _a _few years .ago proved the great mass of the community to be but dupes in the hands of .unprincipled, scoundrels, who filled their pocketsj with the proceeds of immorality, robbery and even murder, committed with the connivance and sanction of 'the police authorities, under a system ofblackmail which has had no parallel in modernj. oivilisation. The populace were groaning _under itheraippression, and an awakening has takenZplace which should d° much to raise private and public morals to a much higher tone. The immediate cause of the revulsion which has led to the overthrow of the evil, so far possession in high places is concerned, may ba found in the fact that thelsystein of TammanY administration had reached the reductio absurdum of the autocratic principle upon which it had been,built up. The principle was that of huge machine,2perfect and complete in all itS parts working without scruple of conscience for the advance to political preferment and publie office of those who were prepared to pay for it, and recoup themselves by fair means or foul out of the public purse. The machine was controlled by one man, Boss CROKER, whose shrewdness and precision were only equalled by his unscrupuloile loess; and for many years it has had the election of New York, city and State, at its disposal. B'S., cently, however, Boss CROKER seems to have tire of the turmoil, and, perhaps, of the unsalutarine,ss of his occupation, and canae:tolEngland to enjol a measure of retirement The ruling passion t°, control would not permit him to give up the reins °I government, and the attempt to play the dictat° at such a distance seems to have introduced weak- ness and discord into the component parts of the charmed ring. He played a bold game when he went over to America a few months ago to take control of the machine on the spot. Not only wee the huge system of criminal corruption, fraud and blackmail which New York citizens had been figh- ing with the energy of a life-and-death struee homologate and fortified, but a nominee Was forward for: the vacant judgeship in t" disreputable ex-Mayor VAN Wvox, whose elec.- tion would have damaged fatally the reputtse: tion of the Supreme Court of the St 11 g, The very grossness of the daring policy Tyll'e sought to place a corrupt judge at the head °I reseed.: demoralised police force has stung every able citizen into action, and the election roretan;" which have now come to hand, are the rep made by an exasperated people. It was deroils development of fortune, unseen by the into. a strange agent who made it possible, that the Presinen'
