chair should now be occupied by one possessing the force of character and the record of Colonel ROOSEVELT. He has shown, by extending the hand of brotherhood to the black-skinned African citizen, how he contemns conventionality; he is hated and feared by the Tammany clique, and if there is condign punishment to be meted out to those who have criminally abused the public trust he is the man to see it done. Under his firm and forceful regime, it may be hoped that Tammany has seen the beginning of the end.
The teachers of the Lon- The London School don School Bpard have Board and their Teachers. had a meeting under the auspices of the Metro-

Politan Board Teachers' Association, and they have expressed their opinion on the strictures which were recsntly made in the annual report of the Board's Inspectors on the class of teaching 130va given at the Bard' s schools. In moving a solution on the subject Mr J Litt, an ex-presid- 'ent of the association, blamed the Board's inspoc- tors: forbronouncing an opinion on a ' test so raeagre as one applied to thirteen schools. Most People will consider the number not a bad asnaple, even considering the large number of schools carried on by the Board. But in explain- ing and justifying the position of the teachers Mr LT gives away his case against the inspectors. In endeavouring to blame the inspectors and the School Board he owns up to nearly all that

the inspectors have reported against the schools, and describes the situation with no lack °f graphic language. He asserts that pre- tentiousness is encouraged by the Board at the expense of thoroughness. Teachers who sought promotion were frequently asked; "How many children have you in the upper standards ?" " What:specifics do you take in your school ?" "How many scholarships has your school won ?" The bearing of such inquiries is, of
course, self-evident, but it may be questioned Whether it is fairly stated by Air. LITT when he says a teacher appeared to please the Board most Who won a few scholarships with half-a-dozen

_ bright children, even if it involve 's the partial heglect of 300 or 400 others. It is difficult to see Why the bright children may not be encouraged, as they ought to be, without sacrificing the others Who are mediocre; but if this is the interpretation the teachers have put upon their orders, it is Practically admitting that an abuse has crept in, Just in the direction which the inspectors have pointed out. Mr. LITT says he knows schools where the time of the head- master or an assistant was mainly spent with a few children in the sitting-room,

cramming them for local scholarships; and as long as the Board encouraged its teachers to do this the teachers w Juld try to give satisfaction by teaching algebra to boys who could not do arith- Inetic, and French to those who do not know t-Auglish. The Teaching Staff Committee, he says, Must take the responsibility for the present want of thoroughness, which he declares is owing to the numerous additions which have of late years been Made to the curriculum. But the blame is clearly neither that of the Staffa)mmittee, nor the School Board, nor the inspectors, but of the system Which has been introduced at Whitehall, with the deliberate aim of making the work more

varied and pleasant—and certainly easier— both to the pupils and teachers. If in he process the ease and pleasure have come to predominate unduly, and appearance has t4en the place of theroughness, as now seems to be admitted, either the system wants mending Or the teachers are at fault in the practical form In Which they work it out. Strangely enough, -11 r. LITT admits that it'is quite possible to have inost of the ornamental work without sacrificing the..thoroughness of the foundation, and the in- seems to be left that the fault rests with ills own profession, ;in the superficial manner in Wnich they have interpreted their duty. In any 718 W of the case, it is evident that the Bard's inspectors have done a useful, though, it may Os, aa ungrateful, task in c ailing attention to the dan- ger Which threatens our primary education, and it is the duty of all concerned, instead of attempt- ing to shirk responsibility in the matter,to address themselves to the task of providing and applying remedy.

Lord Rosebery has at last consented to take the first step towards leaving the position of solitude Whi hhe had allotted to himself, and has con- sented to give his views on the political situation °nee more. Not this time to a select circle of friends or a section of a party, but to the Liberals Of the county of Derby, assembled at Chesterfield, ono the invitation of their respective Liberal uncils. It has been the opinion, constantly ex- pressed by a few wise seers of the signs of the times, that Lord Rosebery could not permanently efface himself, that his retirement must be tem- porary, and only a time of waiting for further and more effective action when the opportune moment arrived. This is what is happening. Events are now proceeding at such a pace that no one with any claim to patriotic feel- ing, and having things to say which the public ought to learn, could stand aside dumb and un- demonstrative. It is worthy of remark, however, that what the satire and abuse of his critics could not accomplish has been done by a genial and Bympathetic invitation, coming from those who really desire to know what kind of guidance his lordship has to offer to honest Liberals at the pre- sent crisis. Lord Rosebery does not promise 7nuch ; he does not seem to think he can yet be of much use. But he is willing to put his opinions into the common stock, and it may be that these find more candid treatment and a more gener- ous reception than those which a short time ago he committed to public review.

l'Ntany schemes for the invasion of England by the French have been framed, and one or two have been attempted, with disastrous results to the would-be invaders. There have also been our 'ewe scares, best represented, perhaps, by the imaginative accounts of various battles of Dor- king. Our opponents in these affairs, however, are always our lively neighbours across the Channel, and it seems hardly yet to have been realised that Gormany could under certain cir- cumstances, land on Englishysoil an army so formidable that to place against it mere thousands of half-trained mea, whether bearing the name of the 3rd Army Corps or not, would be little less than criminal. A pamphlet by Baron von Edel- sheim now gives some indication of the German view of British vulnerability, and the conclusions are such as, while inculcating watchfulness, need certainly cause no alarm. It is admitted that in a war b'etween England and Germany the naval might of the former would tell, so soon as British ships could be brought back from places where they could be spared ; but it is hardly to be doubted that by a sudden and unex- pected attack Germany could hold the North Sea rtag enough for the landing of eighty or a hundred witinsand men on the east coast. It is then as certain that a naval concentration would cut off e invaders from communication with the Father- ih alit:band, after South African experiences, we do not share the Baron's belief that a march on Lon- don, even though for the moment slightly inferior ores would opposa them, would be an easy task

for the invaders, while anything else would mean extermination. As in the case of a French raid, our strength should lie, first, in the ovewhelming power of the navy; and, secondly, in the presence of a well-trained, if small, home army ready for immediate mobilisation. It is the duty of our military and naval reformers to see to it that at all costs these essentials are maintained or secured.

Mr It A Naylor is an involuntary exile from his home at Grappenhall. When it is stated that his place of exile is the pleasantly-situated Welsh -watering place with the Welsh-sounding name of Pwllheli many, perhaps, will be more disposed to envy the exile than to pity him. Notwithstand- king this, Mr Naylor feels his position keenly. The insanitary condition of the neighbourhood in which his home is situated has caused him to leave it as a means of self-protection, ' and until the nuisance is removed he will not again dwell under the roof of Cuerden Hall. The reason for such a step is a grave reflection upon the administrative capacity of the Runcorn Rural District Council. That such a condition of affairs should exist at the beginning of the twentieth century does not say much for our progress in sanitation. Mr Naylor is fortunate in being able to get away from the nuisance but what can be said for the people who are fated to remain in such an unfortunate posi- tion ? They will have to "grin and bear "it whilit the Rural Council with its slow-moving machinery takes steps to remedy a state of affairs which ought to have been set right at least a year ago.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

It is a far cry to Penzance, although the pleasant and thriving Cornish centre is not outside the Eng- glish provinces, and nos too distant to hear there- from the remarkable statement that important experiments are being made in its vicinity " by experts representing influential capitalists, in con- nection with a scheme for extracting gold from sea- water." May they succeed, will be the first words that rise to the lips of some readers, followed by efforts of the imagination to grasp the possibilities which may be expected to accrue. The process is simplicity itself. You simply precipitate the sand by means of lime, extract the gold. and there you are! Of course, it would ill become the laity in such matters to question or doubt the possibility of science, and the time may yet come when Swift's " sunshine from cucumbers" will be regarded as perfectly feasible. The possibilities suggested by the Penzance report may suffice for the present, although sunshine from any kind of vegetable, or anywhere, would ba very agreeable just now as tending to relieve us of the November fogs. But it would be simply grand, and grandly simple per- naps, to run down to New Brighton and pick up a sovereign in a bucket of sea-water on the margin of the golden sands. The rush to the sea-shore will now be greater than ever, and Socialists will have to add the nationalisation of the sea to their present land nationalisation projects, though room ought still to be spared for municipal enterprise. The public, through their Corporation, and no private individual, should reap the benefit of all the gold that can be extracted from every tide that flows up the Mersey. But before saying anything further, one must await, however, auxiously, the receipt of the next report.

It is not surprising to find that in at least one provincial town a dead-set is now being made against the ever present Children's Perambulator on the part of street pedestrians. In trying to avoid Scylla in the shape of the scorching cyclist of the road, the busy pedestrian is always in danger of striking Charybdis ia the form of a glori- ously unconscious nurse girl on the pavement, looking the other way, with a " pram " as she calls it, in front of her. But a committee ot the Ips- wich Corporation assert that there is no legal right to drive baby carriages on the footpath at all, and that this being the case legal proceedings will in future be taken against persons causing an obstruc- tion with such vehicles. One of the consequences of the warning now issued by the Corporation to this effect is, that inasmuch a 3 the electric tram is about to be introduced, mothers of the infantile occupants of such carriages are in a state of alarm, uttering vigorous protests as perhaps only mothers can. Meanwhile members of other corporations are looking on and wondering what the end of it maybe.

It would now appear that another big Coal Strike is at hand. From what was said in thisl letter last week it will be correctly gathered that this refers to the recent developments in South Wales. The Welsh coalfield is believed by those, best able to judge accurately the present situation there, to be upon the eve of another serious stop- page. In 1898 the fruitless struggle which took place lasted five months,and so far as the points in dispute were concerned, left the men in no better position than it found them. This is a matter which does not simply affect one part of the country, but must have a depressing effect upon the neighbouring counties and throughout the Eng- lish provinces. The public of those parts immedi- ately concerned learned with consternation on Monday that the leaders of the coal miners had ordered another stoppage for Wednesday last; making the fourth within a fortnight. The order affected about 150,000 miners of Glamorgan and Monmouth. But there was more in this policy than appeared on the surface; for not only were the men by this act metaphorically snapping their lingers at the coalowners' resolution of last week to prosecute, but have created a situation far more serious than that implied in the defiance of a legal process: From this action of the men's representa- tives in its relation to the sliding scale it became clear that they believe the time has come for the long feared struggle for a minimum wage. In another twelve month or so, when the sliding scale agreement approaches to an end the earnings ' ot the men will probably be much lower than at present, and a prolonged strike following on lean times would not find much favour with the wage earners. This disadvantage, however, does not press now that the colliers have enjoyed a year or more of unexampled prosperity,and,having made up their minds, or had them made up by others, that a struggle in respect of the minimum wage is inevit- able, there is every pronability of the existing situation being allowed to ripen into a crisis forth- with.

--- Provincial Cyclists who travel by rail should read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest what is told in'one of this week's issues of the " Times," A railway porter had charge of a passenger's luggage including a tricycle, and the latter was left some- what close to the edge of the platform. A Rau- chaster express came along at high speed, causing the tricycle to move nearer. Then one of the wheels was nipped off,while other fittings flew in all direc- tions. A " bike " is, of course, not so apt to make a bee line for the train as the tricycle did, but when propped carelessly against a pillar, as it may be seen any day both at railway stations and else- where, the possibilities are great, and sometimes interesting to ponder over .

Smokers who use the tramway cars of the Lon- don County Council have been notified to occupy I only the back seats outside. Provincial tramway and omnibus companies might be expected to " cOpy " such a regulation. As matters stand at present, the ladies prefer the back seats, 'leaving mere man to face and brave the wind, as perhaps he ought to, in order to take the edge off! Mothers at home in the English provinces are certainly interested in the work carried on by the Guild of Loyal Women in South Africa, which has done and is still doing its best to identify and care for the graves of the brave men, whether Britons or Boers, who have fallen in the war. A circular, just issued, sets forth that the many inquiries and the grateful and touching letters received from the relatives of those who have fallen, on learning that the graves dear to them have been located and are being cared for, assure the committee that this work is not only one ot honour to the dead heroes of the war, but it is of real comfort and help to the living. It will, of course, be readily understood that much labour and expense are entailed in the work, and that further funds are needed. Like ; everything else of the kind, at home or abroad money is necessary to carry it on, and money will be cheerfully forthcoming where relatives and friends know that it is properly and promptly laid • out. Though the work appeals chiefly to senti- ment, it is a sentiment old as the hills, and as humanity itself. In ancient times the word piety

div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY NOVEMBER 8 1901. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

was closely associated with the duty of honouring the burying place of ancestors, and in its modest way the Guild of Loyal Women, by respecting a sentiment common to friend and foe alike, is cluing a work that is both pious and politic. If men who go out to fight their country's battles are assured beforehand that their remains,if the worst happens will thus be cared for, they will go and fight with the stouter hearts for it.

, HOSPITAL ACCOMMODATION. -A REMINDER FROM THE LOCAL 4IOVERN3IENT BOARD.

Mr. Thomas Kites assistant secretary to the Local Government Board wrote as follows under date 25th ' October, 1901. Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to advert to your letter of the 9th inst. requesting their sanction to the payment by the Rural District Council of Runcorn of the sum of £3 12s. 4d. in respect of expenses incurred in connec- tion with the nursing of a case of enteric fever in the patient's own home. lam directed to point out that as long ago as the 24th February 1899, the Board stated that they trusted that the Council would take steps to provide antable hospital accommodation for the dis- trict witl.out further delay. In these circumstances the Board are not prepared to give any sanction which would have the effect of withdrawing any frequent pay- ment made by the Connell in respect of the expenses in question from the auditor's jurisdiction. The Clerk said that on receiving the letter he again wrote to the Local Government Board pointing out the exazt circumstances in connection with the hospital. Be had asked them to re-consider the account but had not yet received any reply. Mr Linaker said that he had sent all the necessary papers respecting the hospital site to London and ex- pected to have the draft of the contract down every day. Be had given his consent about the land and was wait- ing for the trustees before laying ,the offer before the [authorities.

' be committee recointnends that the question of provid- ng public baths bd. deferred for the present. Mr. Lightburn in moving the adoption of the minute said that the committee thought it better to defer the matter. At some future time when the bathe would be erected he would have pleasure in calling upon Mr. Pcsaett, for the Elighfield tannery company, Mr. Taylor and the other gentlemen who had promised to contri- bute towards the scheme. Mr Bisbrown seconded. _ .

Mr Taylor was sorry the scheme had fallen through. The question had been before the public many years, and it had long been a grievance that they had no baths The market was a white elephant and be was sure it could be turned to better account. _ _

Mr Icnison thought the matter should not be allowed to drop. It would not be opposed to the will of the people if they tried to provide baths and even if they had to bear their portion of the expense. Be moved that the minute be referred back to the committee.
On Mr. Imison's amendment being put it was unani- mously carried.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY A CORRESPONDENT] The Runcorn Wakes have come and gone. To- day (Friday) the town has resumed its usually quiet appearance and calmly pursues the even tenour of its way, free from the braying of steam-drums, the shrieks of machine whistles, the racket of hobby horses, the frantic yelling of leather-lunged show- men and the jubilant shouts of school boys. Truly such a set of discordant noises is enough to drive those who:dwell in the vicinity of the fair ground in- to the wildest throes of despair! It is,however, one of Runcorn's annual fetes and possesses the dis- tinction of being ancient and honourable. More- ' over, comparatively speaking, it stays here but a short time so that inconvenienced persons have not an unnecessarily protracted spell of misery. Instinctively the Wakes with its interminable gorgeously painted shows, cocoa-nut shies,shooting galleries, swing boats, cheap ware stalls, and last, but by no means least, the everlasting hobby horse recall the once Merrie England of ours where the lads and lasses clad in quaint costumes plaited the may-pole to the sound of flute, tabor and fiddldon the village green. It is from this custom dating long before the time of "Good Queen Bess" from which the present " fairing-day " descends, The townsfolk evidently appreciate this hardy annual, and, judging by the crowds which wended their way to the fair ground there is every reason to believe that a good brisk trade was carried on by the proprietors of the various novelties.

- - Tbere is another auu per uve more widespreed custom closely allied to the above mentioned fete. The anniversary of gunpowder plot has long been a fascination to the juvenile mind and even adults have not been ashamed to speculate in a box of crackers to keep green the frustration of Guy Fawkes. denerally speaking the custom seems to be slowly dying out:and.is perhaps equally as much honoured in the breach as in its observance. The local vendors have, however, plied a brisk trade this season which doubtless accounts for the many miniature explosions heard in the highways and by- ways of the town. It is very pleasing to notice that the children at the Work- house are not forgotten in the general cracking of fireworks. Some kind Warrington gentleman sent quite a large parcel for the edifica- tion of the children housed at Dutton. Doubtless they were rejoiced at the pyrotechnic display and the donor is to be honoured in his effort to brighten their lives. Could he but have seen their gleeful faces on the sth November he would have truly realized that it was better to give than to receive.

The principal business at the Rural Council was, of course, the " talkee, talkee" arising out, of the alleged nuisance at Thelwall. Though Mr Naylor has gone to fields and pastures new in disgust at the prolonged deliberations of the Council, and the odour which comes and goes like a thief in the night, he has left behind him a proxy who will still issue the daily bulletins re the disposition of the nuisance for the benefit of the Council. Quite 1 a number of letters from various individuals were received to the effect that the virulence of the 'odour had not abated one jot or tittle. In fact,one lady went so far as to say that it had been the direct cause of one of her children contracting diphtheria. It was only after considerable discus- sion that the letters were read,many members being convinced that to read the epistolary communica- , tion was sheer waste of time.

Admiral Jones-Parry as usual was well to the front in the discussion. Determined to find out whether there was any truth in Mr Roylance's re- marks at the last meeting he stated that he had been to the place where the filled up pits lay and had found out that words could not describe the terrible effluvium arising from them. He had also found out that there was a drain running from the pits to Weaste-lane and that in wet weather, when there was an overflow of water, the stench was in- tensified. As a proof that the pits were one mass of fermentation the gallant admiral had courageously run the danger gauntlet of infection and brought a sample of the fungus growing on the top of the pits for the special edification of the Councillors. As this sample considerably irritated the olfactory organs of the members it was taken as a good specimen of what the pits contained. Now that the attention of the Council has been drawn to this matter a thorough investigation should follow to dissipate the fears and alarms which will assuredly arise alter such astounding assertions.

The tradesmen of the town will be pleased to learn that the contracts for the building of the Transporter Bridge are now signed and sealed, and that the work will have to be finished by the 20th June, 1903. Planning has already commenced at Runcorn, and no doubt when tile work gets in full swing it will have the effect, irrespective of the value of the bridge when complete, to livening up the trade of the town.

So far nothing has yet been done towards pro- viding the town with a suitable range of baths. The General Purposes Committee in presenting its report on Thursday at the Council meeting was of opinion that the matter had better be left in abeyance until some future date, but on the amend- ment of Mr Imison, the Council wisely referred the matter back to the committee for further con- sideration. It has been felt fora longtime now among the ratepayers that if there is need of a park there is infinitely more necessity for a range of baths where the youths and adults may learn the "finny art" of swimming. The need is so apparent and so pressing that it is useless to labour the point. One thing is certain the Council will have behind them the unanimous will of the people when they finally decide that baths shall be erected.

FOOTBALL. I was much disappointed with the display against Huddersfield. We won it is true, by seven points to nil, and that fact was very welcome because it meant two points and a further step up the ladder, but victory was 9carcely deserved. It was the most ragged performance I have seen the club do this season, and I hope it was merely a temporary falling from grace. The passing was of the most ordinary description and each back was at fault some time or other in the game.

For a wonder Faukner was as big a sinner as anyone in failing to take his passes, and also in parting rather awkwardly and here the whole source of trouble may have arisen. Here however there is ample excuse. tarly on in the game his knee gave way again, but be refused to leave the ground and pluckily playei to the finish; and the result it is said, is that he will not turn out in another match for three months. This is indeed bad news, for there is no more sterling and clever half back in the Northern Union than Faulkner.

Fortunately the fielding and kicking of the Greens were up to concert pitch, and the forwards, although well matched in the scrimmaze, followed ' up with pertinacity and judgment, and thus gave , the necessary lead. The only try scored reflected great credit upon both Farme, and Williams. Warder's goal was ot a kind seldom seen. Catching the ball on the bounce, be neatly kicked it over the bar, a " flying " answer to a kick by the Hudders- field full back which was not anticipated. Houghton was again in champion form. Jones gave a poor exhibition and he has been deposed for to-morrow's match in favour of Moran, who, it appears, has removedlbis belongings to Warrington.

Runcorn usually rise to the occasion, and a much superior game may be expected at Bradford to-day. A good team has been chosen. Faulkner, of course, will be an absentee, but Richardson will partner Jolley, and this couple are hard to beat, as was seen in the County match. It is to be hoped, however, that Jolley will restrain his kicking propensities, for in this department of the game the Tykes are equal adepts with any Lancashire or Cheshire Club. I am!glad to notice that the "A "team forwards are being given:a chance. Four in Moulton, Williams, Woods and Brookes will figure in to-morrow's match and if the Linnets triumph at Park Avenue, I shall have great hopes of their finishing the season very near No 1, if not l absolute first.

The full team chosen is as follows : Houghton, back; Butterworth, Warder, Wilkinson and Moran, three-quarter backs ; Jolley and Richardson, half- backs; Moulton, Williams,VVoods, Langley,Walker, Farmer, Lightfoot awl Brookes.

div.head: QUESTION OF DRAINAGE.
div.p: A QUESTION OF DRAINAGE.

WON. Davies and Forshaw, Warrington, wrote that II their client Mr. Alfred Clare, of Ivy Mount, Latchford, had temporarily allowed vaiious occupiers aad residents to drain through bis drain on the understanding that the District Council were laying drains. They asked if this was correct. Mr John Swinton, In reply, wrote that he enclosed a plan showing a proposal to divert the present sewer which now existed through Mr Clare's land so as to have it under the road. This scheme,was proposed by Mr. F R Roberts, solicitor, Warrington, and sanctioned oy the Council, but why it was proposed and why it had not been carried out he could not say. Probably Mr. Clare had raised objections to bisdrain. Mr Woodward proposed that inquiries be made into the Case, and a report made to the Council as to their exact position, Carried.
THE tHELWALL WATER SUPPLY.

Mr. James Deas, water and sanitary engineer, Munici- pal Offices. Warrington. wrote under date:2Bth October re the Thelwall water supply, returning plan left by the Council's surveyor with the extensions marked thereon. These would bring up the total cast to £920. The Clerk said tast this statement was in accord- ance with the agreement of the committee. He pro- duced the plan and the agreement with the Warrington :Corporation who would lend the amount, provided a guarantee was given of eight per cent for seven years on the;Corporation's outlay. If the rates did not amount to the eight per cent on ne outlay Um the parish of Tbelwall would have to make it good. The document Was sealed. HATTON SEWAGE. .

The Clerk produced a formal agreement with Sir Gilbert Greene!l for the laying or sewers across certain land in Hatton and according to the resolution giving 53. for the rights of way. THE TEIELWALL NUISANCE. The Clerk said be had received several letters re the above nuisance from different persons to the effect that there was a strong nuisance arising from the brook and tannery, and also one from Mr. Naylor under :lite October 24th, from the West End Hotel, Pwllheli, North Wales, asking (1) if his letter was read at the last Council, and (2) if net, why not. The Clerk having re- plied to these queries, Mr. Naylor wrote as follows on November itch :—Yours of October 25th, 1901, for which I thank you, and wherein you state it was resolved by your Council " that none of the correspond- ence be read." I wish to inform your Council that I protest against such conduct, which only seems to show the public that your Council are still determined to adopt what has been described by the press as "a policy of secrecy and concealment." Mr Wright thought that the other letters should be read. Mr Stokes pointed out that the remon why they were not read before was owing to the matter being in the hands of the Local Government Board. Their reply had been received and the resolution was no longer,binding. The Clerk in reply to s question by Mr Linaker said that the purport of. the letters was that the nuisance still existed. A Couacillor : I should like to hear Mr Long's letter read. Mr Woodward contended it was a waste of time to , read the repetitions contained in the letters. Admiral Jones Parry said that the letter be got the Clerk to read at the last meeting was one of toe best they had yet had. It had only been discovered acci- dentally by him to have been written by the gentleman in question. Mr Woodward opposed it then but his motion was carriel. It was rather a waste of time to wrangle over them being read than to rean them, Mr Linaker asked whether any of them would throw light on the diffieult position they were In ? Mr Spruce said there was an impression abroad that the Council was treating the affair indifferently. They Should therefore be read. The Chairman retorted that he had been told they were making too much of it. After further discussion the following correspond- ence was read after a proposition had been made on the question :—Letters dated October 22nd, 23rd, 24th, 25th, 26:b, 28th, 30th,31st November Ist, 2nd and 4th, from Mr, L. Leah of the Stables, Cuerden Hall, notify- ing the hours on each day when the Stench from the tannery brook in Weaste-lane was the source of annoy- ance and nuisance. Messrs William Long and Son Grappenhe 11, War- rington, wrote under date October 24th advising the Clerk that Monday the 28th ult. would be suitable for an interview. That morning their attention was called to a repetition of the strong sewage smell emanating from the two pipes on the 'nide/all side of the culvert similar or worse than, when the Council's deputation first attended there accompanied by Drs Vacher and Adams when doubtless you remember we wired Dr Adams at Antrobus at once, but on his arrival soon after noon the flood water bad so much increased that it was no use his taking samples. A neighbour, however, passing at the earlier period, can ispealt to its nauseous condition. Mr L W Reynolds, Millington House, Thelwall, wrote under date October 28th. Nuliance at Grappenhall. A friend of mine has asked rue whether my recent letter to the Council was read at the last meeting. I Could not tell him anything except that it was riot reported in the press. If the letter was read perhaps you would kindly let me know. Mrs Sarah Ann Quennell, Cuerden-place, Weaste-lane, Tbelwall, wrote complaining of the nuisance at the tannery brook, and alleging that her children had been taken ill in consequence. Mr Mclntyre said that during the whole of the time the letters had been written the wind was in the south east and yet thoughlMr Naylor' premises lay east of the tannery they caught the odour. This was a most ex- traordinary thing. If it arose from the road it would take it away in a contrary direction altogether. Admiral Jones-Parry declared that he had at least found out the true cause of the stench It lay in the pits discovered be' Mr 103-1 ince. The overflow from them came into Weaste-lane. He submitted a plan showing the exact position of them. Three years ago Mr Long made a new " rua " from cum of those pits of the tannery into the drain. Ee asked the medical officer if he knew anything about these pits. The Medicalpfficer • No Ido not ! Admiral Jones Parry : There is very lax duty on the part of the Medical Officer of Health. The Medical Officer : 1 wish to retract my observa- tion then. I want to know exactly where they lie. Admiral Jones earry said they were situated three quarters of a mile up the Kontsford-road near the cottage of a gamekeeper named Hankinson. The new drain came, right through the pit and he was told under the tannery. The new drain he bad seen for himself. He believed it was an illegal act to build that drain. The stench was always there when there was an overflugh of water. He had brought samples with him from the pits which were under the table. Unfortunately the smell lead escaped. (Laughter.) ' Mr. Linaker said he coulci not agree with the censure passed on the Medical Officer of Health. He only hoped the bulk of the pits weuld be up to Admire! Jones Parry's sample. Complaints had been received when , there had been no rains. Na doubt the pits contributed' to and intensified the odour. What was the material with which the pits had been filled up? Mr. Mclntyre said he had visited the pits and there I was no perceptible smell. He had seen the tenants on whose land the pits lay and they had told him there was no nuisance and that on the pits they grew some of their best celery. They were merely filled up with Lark pure and simple. Mr Roylance differed with hie friend. They were not filled up with bark only but with other matter. Thera was a fungus growth on the top. and there was an abominable smell. Every one keew that celery thrived better on manure than anything else. B &TS FOR RUNCORN. SUDDEN DEATH.. OF A CHILD AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday afternoon at the Runcorn Police Court an inquest was held, touching the death of a child named Blanche Gayter by Mr Dobson coroner. Mr Miller was the foreman of the jury. Thomas Gayter, 16, Carrm-street stated that the deceased was his child and. was seven months old. She had been a weakly child from her birtn but was in good health on the day of her decease. She slept with her two sisters on Mon- day night. The girl who had charge of the child was 17 years of age. Witness called his daughter Gertrude to get up at 6.30 a.m. After dressing herself she went to the foot of the bed where the child lay and found her dead. She called witness who went upstairs and found the body quite cold.—Dr W Bethune deposed that he had known the child from birth. She was very weakly. He was called by the last witness to see the child. He bad made a post-mortem examina- tion of the body and found the body very poorly nourished. As a result of the examination he believed that the child had died from convulsions probably due to teething. There was no suspicion of over-lying.—A verdict in accordance with the medical evidence was returned.

div.head: SCHOOL BOARD ELECTON,
div.p: THE SCHOOL BOARD ELECTON,
RUNCORN.

Bath sides are now working with the utmost vig- our.On Monday evening the Voluntaryist party held a private meeting at which arrangements for the campaign were made. It is now definitely certain that they will not run five candidates as was rumoured but will seek to re-elect the same four who were successful on the last election. Canvass- ing by both sides is being freely done and the electorate may expect to have a most unquiet time of it until the election is over. So far no public meetings have been held by the Volun- ' taryist party, the platform as yet having been resorted to by the Progressives only There is every prospect that the next three weeks will see an unwonted amount of activity among the ratepayers. The election, it is stated will take place on Wednesday the 27th November. This is an awkward day especially for the watermen but it will have the advantage of enabling the trades- men to throw in their energies on the side to which they belong. The local Wesleyan Circuit Magazine in the, course of an article on the forthcoming .School Board election in Runcorn says :—" The future is full of peril to the Board School system, next year changes of a drastic character will be made, and it is of vital importance therefore that all Boards shall be held by strong men who will not readily let slip advantages already won, nor allow the system to be mutilated for the benefit of clericalism. Toe progressive cause is championed by five men, who are foremost in whatever effects the best inVrests of the town. They will not pander CO the low and mean in human nature with such an ignoble cry as " Down with the Rates," but will rather help their townsmen "To rise ors stepping stones " Of their dead-selves to higher things." Largest of ratepayers themselves. toey may be trusted to get full value for every penny of public money spent. They work hard for our trade, the surest way of reducing rates. With employment in our streets and property well tenanted,financial difficulties will speedily vanish. For these and other cogent reasons they satisfy the conditions laid down by our Conference, and we call on all Methodists to work in every honorable way to secure their election."

Canon Wood on the School Board Election In the Runcorn Parish Magazine, the Vicar, the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, M.A., writes as folllws :—" I would give a good deal to avoid a contest at the Coming School Board election, but as I am informed there is no possibility of so doing it remains only for me to ask you all to do your very best for the good cause, and to do that best in the kindliest way you know."
The Progressive Candidates. As previously advertised a meeting will be held in suppott of the Progressive party in Brunswick School- room this (Friday) evening at 7.30.

The monthly meeting of the Council was held on Thursday morning in the Council Chamber. Present Mr R H Posnett J.P. (in the chair) Messrs D Bisbrown, Handley, J H Saltkeld, E Imison, T W Jones, J Pritchard. div.head: PARK QUESTION AGAIN.
div.p: THE PARK QUESTION AGAIN.

- The Highways and Buildings Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. William Moore, Runcorn, f work to be done in connection with the turning over of soil, leveling, &z., at the Common, in accordance with specification, be accepted; that seed be purchased for the Common at an estimated cost of £3O. The Committee reported that Sir John T Brunner had offered through the Chairman of the Cosncil to provide trees and labour to the value of £5O. the trees to be planted in the public roads and streets of the town, and that he be thanked for his offer and that the offer be accepted. It was recommended that a Committee, con- sisting of the Chairman of the Ccunei', the Chairman of the Highways Committee, the Chairman of the Finance Committee, and Mr Handley. be authorised to plant trees at such places as they may fix upon, the chairman hay- ing given a guarantee that the trees would be provided and the work done without entailing any charge on the rates.
Mr Taylor movAd the adoption of the minutes, and said that the £3O for plants did not include the roa,-i- -way.. _
ir Pritehard sP,coaded.

Mr Biabrown moved as an amendment that the minutes relating to the turning over of sod to the purchasers of seed be deleted, and that the question of further expen- diture on the common be postponed for twelve months.l This matter had been before them several times. They would remember that in 1899 a resolution was passed in favour of borrowing £4,000 with a view to providing a pleasure ground. There had been fuither developments since then and it was now termed a park. The last time it was before them in July 1900. they had decided to spend up to that the £2,200 which the Council had authorized for the draining of ithe Common and making roads, etc. Hi 3 point was that the amount already spent of the £2,200 should have been ample for the purpose to provide a pleasure ground. It was not necessary to complete the scheme. The impression then given was that there was no inten- tion of going further for • number of years. The amount spent was quite sufficient for a long time t ) come. Now they were proposing to spend £250 more in addition to £3O. Tells meant a total expenditure of £3,354. If they went on like this rates would go up instead of being reduced. He wished simply to save expenses. Be had no objection of providing a park,but enough money had already been spent. Mr. Salkeld seconded the amendment. He believed the town could not afford the money which would be spent. He voted for the £l,OOO being spent in July but Ihe would not have done so had be known it would be

followed with a considerable amount of further expendi- ture. This was the expressed intention of several of the members. Mr. Salkeld quoted extracts from many of the members speeches at that meeting to the effect that no 1 further money would be required. Continuing the speaker said it was a very strange thing that they now had a proposition to spend £3OO more. He had can- vassed the ratepayers he repre.Feated and:the feeling was that the Council should practice economy with respect to the scheme. Shortly toey would require perhaps one or two persons to look after the Park, and this would be a permanent burden on the rates. They should eon- eider whether it was not best to study economy, seeing the bad trade of the tcwo.

Grice supported tbe amendment. His opinion had been that it would be advantageous to secure tbe land by making the road to Rock Savage, and that furtber expenditure would be met in the course of time. It would be an advantage to the ratepayers to stop the expense, and to leave the matter in abeyance twelve months.

Mr Lightburn said they would be in the same position in twelve months as then. He lived on the spot and saw the multitude of p-ople who made use of the park. If they did not spend the amount it would keep idle the money already spent.

4. Mr WiSwall said if it was postponed for twelve months it would be twelve months lost. Part of that common wanted dealing with at once, and should be made into a place for the youths to enjoy. The money should be spent but additional expenditure should be seriously considered. It would be a mistake if they did not finish what they had begun. With respect to canvassing he was convinced that nine- tenths of the people would receive with open arms what they bad done. Mr Taylor said that his peaition had always been that they should drain the common and make it fit for a playground. They had left the making of the p!ay- ground until the last instead of doing it before. If they did as Mr Bishrown suzgested a lot of the work would be undone and would be required to be done again. In voting for the minute he did so simply b4:cause they were going to do what should have beeo done at first. Mr Taylor, in reply to the various speakers, said they had long been discussing the question but ultimately they bad decided to apply to the Local Government Board for Dower to spend £4,000. They had spent £2,200, £1,200 of which had ben spent on roads which had been for years and years a dis.lraco to Runcorn. They had also the draining to do with a portion of that money. To leave the scheme at that point would be a ridiculous thing and they would make a laughing stock of themselves. He ridicaled the idea of the ratepayers being canvassed. The large ratepayers like the Ship Canal Company, the United Alkali, etc., did not object to provide for the children of Rua-

corn a' pink and play ground. He was sorry 1 that any member of the Council should stand in the way of providing pleasure grounds far the young people and adults. Nambers of young children were brought before the magistrates for playing In the streste. Woo were to blamo ? Not the children but the authori- ties. It was their duty to provide facilities of this kind and he could not think that Messrg Bisbrown. Grine and S iltkold were in earnest over the matter. If the town were properly canvassed there would be a large majority in favour of the scheme. Personally he was not so narrow minded as to refuse a play ground to the people. Ile urged the Council to take a sound and proper view of the matter. Mr. Grico explained that he was not opposed to the scheme at all. Ile merely advised that the whole of the expenditure should not be gone into at one time. The voting taking place, four voted for the amend- ment and ten against. the minutes being duly carried. THE SLAUGHTER-ROUSE. THE COUNCIL AND THE CO—OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The Health Committee reported that the sub-corn_ mittee appointed to inspect the public slaughter-house, with a view of ascertaining if there was sufficient accommodation for the slaughtering cf pigs were of opinion that all the present and immediate Future requirements of the town would be mtt by the fixing of a winch, the provision of a fat board ad- ditional fixtures for the suspending of carcases, ad- ditional water to supply boilers, repairs to tunnel and the laying of a bed of concrete under the fine, The committee also reported that it had again considered the application of the Runcorn Co-operative Society for permission to kill pigs at the rear of their premises Churcb-street,and recommended that the Society be in- formed that in face of bye-law No. 1 any licence granted would be void. Mr Dean moved and Mr Jones seconded the adoption of the minute.

Mr Imison asked could any information be given aR to the expenditure involved in carrying out the recom- mendations of the sub-Committee ? Mr Dean, in reply, stated that Mr Wilding had esti- mated the cost at about£s. The concreting of the floors was a scheme that was intended to have been carried out previous to the visit of the sub committee After further discussion the minutes were approved.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

The Northern Union and Northern League meetings were held on Tuesday evening, and some important business was transacted. Most interesting of all was the charge against Oldham and Hunslet of brealdng Professional Law 2. Both cases were proved and small fines inflicted on the offending clubs. At the next meet- ing of the Northern League Oldham and Hunslet wil/ have two points deducted according to rule. There will then be five of the fourteen clubs on the same footing as regards penalties.

Warrington have chosen the following team to do duty at St Helens to-day :—llallam, full-back ; Rat- chile, Isherwood, Dickenson and Harris, threequarters ; Allen and Hockenhall, half-backs ; Boardman, Morri- son, Eden, Fell, Edmondson,J Swift,F Swift and Jolley. forwards,

Fish will be an absentee owing to his injury last Saturday, which turns out to be more serious than was expected. The popular left winger has broken a bone in the back of his hand and will probably be out of the field for three weeks at least. This means that he will also miss the county match with Yorkshire against whom he was anxious to play. Hard luck for Fish, for Warrington and for Lancashire!
Boardman is said to be all right again so he comes on the team vice Cunningham. I hope his knee will stand the test for a 14 stony man like Boardman is much missed in the scrimmage.
Harriers.

Warrington Athletic Club held their first annual novice race on Saturday last. The course selected was about four and a half miles in length all on the road and eight runners started. A splendid race ensued,the first four being all together a quarter of a mile from home, and resulting in W Brown winning by about 10 yards from C Whittaker, who was about the same dis- tance in front of J Jump. To-day Warrington have Runcorn Harriers as visitors. The race is from. IL Ashton's, Bridge Inn, at 3.30 p.m,

Earlestown Harriers visited Warrington on Saturday for the inter-club run with Sankey Harriers. Excel- lent weather for cross-country running prevailed, and as a result there was a large muster. It was decided to count the first four in each team. The pack num- bered 40, made up of 31 Sankey and nine of the visi- tors. A start was made about 3-30, when the pack, paced by G Eastwood and whipped in by L Green (San- key), went off at a quick pace in the direction of the Bold estate. About six miles of grand country had been traversed when the party lined up for the dash home. J Wilding, S Parsonage (Sankey), and G Halton Earles- town) immediately made headway, followed closely by Potts and Devlin. About 300 yards from home a stiff race was witnessed between L Green, J Wilding, S Par- sonage and T Devlin, all of Sankey, the latter eventu- ally winning grandly by about ten yards. The follow- ing are the positions of the counters :—Sankey : T Devlin, 1; S Parsonage, 2 ; J Wilding, 3; L Green, 4.; total, 10 points. Earlestown : G Halton, 7; J W Ellison, 11 ; J Walton, 13; and E Lewis, 18 ; total 49 points. The home team thus won easily by 39 points. Two of the club's badges were offered as an encourage- ment to the novices for the first two home, and were won by P Wilding and J Watson.

FendaY—Before Mr Hepherd (in the chair). Councillor Smethurst and John Roberts add Mr Thornton. Darts iv ON LICENSED PREmISEs. —Jam es Quigley. 25. Naylor Street and John Morren, 30, James btreet, were charged with being drank and refusing to quit the "Alexandra" Vaults. Scotland Road, on October 27th.— William Adams Ray, the landlord, said the defendants came into the public house drunk and Le refused to serve them aed told them to go home. They woul I not go out and witness. had to obtain assistance. When he came back they bad left the premises but they returned in about an hour and he had much trouble in getting them out.—Defendants. who were both old offenders were fined 20s and costs with the option of a month's imprisonment. SMART FINE Fall BRE•XING A LAMP —Patrick Memnon, 20, Old Road, was charged with doing wilful damage to a lamp, the property of James Archibald Ewart,—Mr Taylor (Messrs Greenall and Company) prosecuted, sad said Mr Bwart was engaged in laying the Corporation tramways at the junction of Mersey Street and Bridge Street. On the evening of October 21st, as usual a number of lamps suspended from poles were lighte fin different places in order to proteet Passengers and traffia. Defendant came down Bridge Street with another young man and deliberately smashed one of the lamps by kicking it.—Defendant was find 5S and costs and ordered to pay the amount of the damage (1 4s 6d Elan). WIFE DESERTION.—John 14eyes. 10 Birchall-street, was summoned for deserting his wife Margaret Heves, Back Orford-lsne.—Complainent said her husband had not elven her any money for ten weeks.—The magistrates granted a separation order with 66 per week alimony. SATITRDIY.—Before Mr T Birchen, Alderman Hea'on,Coun- cillor John Roberts, add Mr H T Fairclongh, Imeenroteen POE THEFT.—Thotnas Carney and Samuel Brans, last from Bolton, were charged with stealing a pair of boots value 2s 6d from the shop of John Gibbons, second- ' hand dealer, Mersey-stteet at 3.30 on Friday afteruiion.— Superintendent Moneghen stated that at 3 p in. on Friday afternoon he and D te.itive Barlow were in Mersey-street and saw the prisoners loitering near Mr Gibbons' shop. Ultimately they came away and he noticed that the first prisoner was carrying a slashing hook and the second prisoner had something bulky under his cost. It was found that a pair of boots were conce sled under Eyans's coat, and on being queationei he said he bad bought them, but ulti- mstely be admitted the thefts It appears that while Carney was offet 'mg the slashing book for sale Rvans purloined the boots. Prisoners said they were in want of food and stole the b ots in order to obtain some —They were each sent to gaol for a month with bard labour. MOND.S.T.—Before Me Monks (in the chair), Alderman Hutchinson, and Messrs Birchen, Hayward, Wright and Thoriaton. PooTßlLL.—Joseph Hughes, 35, Mersey-street, William Poole. labourer, 6 Mersey-street, Harry Cross, 15. Rose and Crown-street, and William Foster. 113, Sharp-street. all youth's, wer, summoned for playing football in Mersey-street on October 25th. Mr Steel appeared on behalf of the defend- ants and pleaded not guilty.—P C Clough said that at 7.30 on Senday evening be', was On duty in Mersey-street near Litton's-row. when he saw the four defendants, with others, kicking a football about the street. He chased the boys and hay.ng caught Hughes obtaine 1 the names and addresses of the others from him. He had had several com- plaints about the disoderly conduct and had cautioned defendants. It was no use telling them, and he himself had witnessed the disorderly conduct several nights.—la answer to witness : He had not had the name of a boy Leslie given him as having been there. —Mr Steel, for the defencr, said that the boys had a field at Arpley where they played football and the defendant Poole bad been repairing the ball. In the evening the other boys came to him and asked him to give them the ball to play with in th 3 field, but he said it was not ready to take out. Eventually they did have the ball and were standing near a window with it when a boy named Leslie came up and knoeked it cut of Hughes's hand. A man who waS Musing kicked the ball and the defendants ran after it Clough same up and they ran away. Defendants never kicked the bid' at all.—The Chairman maid the Bench considered the Case proved and the boys would be fined 5s each,

She had previously obtained a separation with an order of 6s weekly. but had cohabited with him again owing to his promise of reform. He earned £1 a week. Three weeks ago be turned her out one cold night and refused to maintain her.—Defendant pleaded not guilty and alleged misconduct by his wife. Defendant, in Curt. used very foul lansuage towards his wife, and was warned that he would be proceeded against for contempt of court.—Ultimately defendant was ordered to pay 6s weekly. the mother to have charge of the child. Weston Point, were charged with tress- passing on land in search of game and having in their possession six rabbits, and instruments for taking game on the 31st October—P.C. Rowlands stated that on the date named he saw the two defendants near the hospital at Higher Runcorn, In the possession of Darlington he found six rabbits, a line sixty eigkt yarels long, seven pegs and one bludgeon. The other defendant had one dog line, and one bludgeon When questioned by witness they admitted the offence.—Fi•ned 40. and Is 6i costs each. Warrington Church Society. The first lecture of the series in connection with the above Society was given in the Co•operative Hall on Monday evening by the Rev R F G Smith- wick, vicar of r•eaforth, who took for his subject " An hour in Palestine, a talk about the Holy Land" Mr U S Burgess presidei Over a large audience. —The Chairman, in the course of his introductory remarks said the subje.c;: of the lecture was one which could not fail to be attractive to every one in the room, especially if there were any present who, like himt,elf, had had an opportunity of visit- ing Egypt and Pdlestine, about which places they were to hear that evening. He could tell the audience a good many stories about the things he saw when he was there, but, of course, it would be out of place to do so in the circumstances —The lec- ture was then proceeded with and proved highly in- teresting.lt wasillustrated with beautiful limelight views, the lantern being manipulated. by Mr H N Houghton. Commenting upon Nazareth, the lec- turer said that it was tne most fascinating village in the whole of the Holy Land, and a view was shown of a spot where the lecturer and his com- pany camped for the night at an altitude of 6,000 feet, Daring the course of the lecture the follow- ing musical selections were given ;—Song, " Naz areth " (Gounodl, Mr T Humphries; "There is a green hill (Gounod), the Parish Church choir boys; and "The Holy City" (Adams), Mr P C Price. Mr Party was the accompanist. The utual votes of thanks terminated the proceedings.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS Al WARRINGTON.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS Al WARRINGTON.
Councillor Ellison Increases his Majority.

The only real contest in the municipal elections at Warrington on Friday was in Latchford Ward.lt will be remembered that at the last moment Mr. S. Gough, who had been nominated as the candidate for tit. John's and Bewsey R ards, withdrew from the field, giving 88 his reason that the retirinp, can- didates, Mr John Baird (St. John's) and Mr W Rogers (Bewsey) had expressed themselves in complete sympathylwith the resolution in regard to no municipal trading,passed at the meeting held on the previous Wednesday at the Co-operative Hall Mr Gough, however, only came to the decision not to conteA the wards, after the legal time limit had , been passed, and consequently the polling booths had to be opened,and the usual expenses incidental to an election, Incurred by the Corporation. In Latchford Ward :,he retiring Councillor. Mr Luke Ellison (L), was oppo!ed by Mr John Pember- ton (C), and in Old; conest the greatest interest was evinced by the townspeople generally. Mr Pemberton although be was the Conservative nominee fought the election on " municipal ' purity "lines. There was a good display of mural literature on both sides, prominence of course being given to the municipal trading. The two polling stations for Latchford Ward were at St. James' School, Old-road, and Christ Church School, Wash-lane. The presiding of-Filers were '—Messrs T Coper. C H timiworth, and W D Jeans, jun., and the poll clerks, Messrs A Wool, J W Howarth and R Hind.

In Bewsey and Sr. John's Wards the polling booths were opened as usual at 8 o'clock, and several voters recorded their votes. No voter appeared after about three minutes past eight, and as there were no signs ot opposition to the retiring candidates the booths were closed at a quarter past nine. The ballot boxes were taken to the Town Hall and the votes were counted with those from Latchford Ward. In Sr John's Ward the presiding officers were Messrs W H J Jenkins, T S Steel and F Timperley and the poll clerks were Messrs A Starkey, Joel Smith, and J Houghton. The presiding officers in Bewsey Ward were Messrs J Smith and W Boyle and the pOl clerks Messrs W T Crank and H P Brierley. During the early part of the day polling in Latchford Ward was rather slow,but towards even- ing it for came brisk, the supporters of both candi- dates working bard to bring voters to the polling booths. At eight o'clock the booths were closed and the boxes were conveyed to the Town Hall where the counting operations took place.
RESULTS OF THE POLL. LATCHFORD WARD. Luke Elligon (L) Jahn Pembarton (C) .......... 506
Majority ....—....—. 77 ST. JOHN'S WARD. John Baird (C) Samuel Gough (I) . . w....... 0 BEWSBY WARD. William Rogers (I) l2
Samuel Gough (i).

There were two spoiled papers. At tie conclu- sion of the counting, Councillor Ellison proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Bolton, the presiding and returning officer of the ward. Mr John Pambertou seonded and the re.,olution was unani- mously agreed to. Alderman Bolton acknowledged the compliment. AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.
Immeliat-ely after the declaration of the poll Mr Ellison'e supporters accompanied him to the Liberal Club, where speeches were delivered.

Councillor'PEscocK announced the result of the election and said the majority was the largest ever attained in Latchford Ward. (Cheers ) He con- gratulated Mr Ellison upon the admirable fight be had made after all the pressure which ha been brought to bear to oust, him from his position as a member of the Council. After Mr Ellison had served the ward for six years he (the speaker) hardly thought it credible that the people of Latch- ford would have turned him out after serving them as be had done. There was not a straighter man in the Council than Mr Ellison. (Cheers). Councillor Ellison, who had a rousing reception, thanked all those who had worked for him very heartily, and he trusted that their labours wool') not be in vain. (A voice : "They have not been." He had endeav ured so far to do his best for the good of the ward. When he entered the Council be found the ward in a very neglected condition so far as streets were concerned, He had made every endeavour to improve this state of things and he thought he had been fairly successful. He should in future do all he could for the prosperity of Latchford and of War- riogton to toe best at his ability. He thanked ! them very heartily for the way in which they had received his name that night. (Cheers). The proceedings then closed. MR PEMBERTON AND THE CONSERVATIVES Speaking at the Conservative Club, Mr Pember- ton said he had not the slightest doubt that if he had received the support of the Conservative Club and the Conservative workers he would have won. (Hear, hear, end applause). When he said the Conservative workers ne meant the heads of the party who ought to rally round them on all occasions of that kind. The only support he had received from the party had been from unofficial members of the ast-o:dation and the club and all those he thanked most heartily, in fact, quite as heartily as if he had won. (Applause).

div.head: SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT LYMM. ---- An Old Lady's Fatal Fall Downstairs.
div.p: SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT LYMM. ---- An Old Lady's Fatal Fall Downstairs.

A shocking accident happened at Bleak House, Lymm, the residence of Mr. John. Burgess, a partner in the firm of Robert Davies and Co., Solicitors, Warring- ton, on Thursday last week, by which Mrs. Louisa Bollans, aged 74, lost her life. The deceased lady was Mrs. Burgess's mother, and resided at The Cottage, Lymm, and on the day in question she went to Mr. I Burgess's house about 11.30 a.m. She was apparently in her usual health, though it should be mentioned that cataract on the eye rendered her almost blind. At 6 o'clock Mrs. Bollans was passing from the nursery to her bedroom and being an active woman she declined the guidance of a maid. She called out "Are you there ?" to Mrs Burgess, wkci, a 'moment later heard a fall and found the de- ceased at the bottom of the upper flight of stairs, quite unconscious. Dr Burrows was called in at once, but Mrs Bollans expired at 9 o'clock the same night.—Mr R Dobson, coroner, held an inquest at Bleak House, on Friday, when the above facts were borne out. Dr Burrows testified that death was due to a fracture of , the base of the skull, and the jury brought in a verdict of "Accidental death," also passing a vote of condo- lence a ith the family and relatives of the deceased ady.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
THE NORTHERN LEAGUE.
A POOR GAITH AT WARRINGTON.

The Wilderepool ground was on Saturday the scene of a poor encounter between Warriakton and Brighouse Rangers the bottom club of the Northern League. Neither side played good football and the 4,003 sp2ctstors present were disappointed. thouzli Warrington won in the end, Fine weather favoured the fixture and tha sides were at full strength with the exception that Baker of Brighouse was Playing threequarter for his county. Mr Renton of Huns- let was the referee and the teams lined out as follows :

Brighouse Rangers : Saville, fall back ; Walker, Booth- royd, Chappell and Hartley, threeguarters ; Denham and Holroyd, half backs; Walton. Weivill, Armitage, Miller, Hodgeon, Byrom. Pearson and Woffenden forwards. Warrington Hallam. full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son. and Harris. threeguarters ; Allen and Hockenhall. halfbacks; Morrison. li/den. Edmondson. Fell, Cunningham, Jolley, J Swift, and F Swift, forwards. The Rangers started and Warrington at once attacked close in. Denham wa penalised for picking out, and Fish planed a goal in the first five minutes. Brighouse immedi- ately rushed to the other end, and Warrington infringing the rules Saville lande i an egualleing goal with a fine shot. Give and take play followed, Warrington holding the upper hand by superior back play, but being bidly beaten In the scrummages. Dickenson brake away, and dodged to the line where he was pulled down by Saville. The latter at last drove Warrington to the other eod by powerful punting, and Walker receiving a pass from the scrimmage dropped at goal, the bill passing outside the posts by the merest trifle Allen and Cunningham were the means of relieving the pressure on the Warrington line. The Rangers were driven back, and Isherwood was almost over after good passing. Saville tried at goal from centre, but missed, and half-time Caine with the score I goal each. 1 J Swift resumed and exchange kicking resulted in War- rington losing ground. The ball was payed out promptly but Dickenson mulled, and at this stage Warrington's play I all round was poor in the extreme. .The Rangers were mu 3h I the more energetic, Bo Ahroyd milting several capital runs. I Harris at last „livened things up by a run three parts the length of the field, having the hardest luck not to score after kicking past Saville. Stimulated by derisive cheers the Warrington forwards roused themselves and the b wks were given opportunities to score which went begging. vista made a fine individual effort but succumbed to numbers. Before Warrington could ba cleared out Pies placed the ball right oa the line from touch and Fell fielding smartly ran in close to the posts. Fish easily landed a goal. The game was now as good as over though the Rangers worked hard. Walker once got away from Deutiam's pass. but kicked dead when challenged. The final came with the score reading : Warrington, two goals one try (seven points) ; Brighouse hangers, one goal two points,)

div.head: RUNC3BN V. HUDDERSI:ELD.
div.p: RUNC3BN V. HUDDERSI:ELD.

The above teams met at Runcorn on Saturday. There was but an average attendance. The ground was In very fair condition and there was no wind. Bath teams were repro• I sentative and Included the following players : Hu corn :Houghton.back ;Jones, Butterworth,Warder, and Wilkinson three-quarters ; Fsulkner and Jolley, halves ; Walker, Farmer, Langey,Lightfoot,Yiroods,Williams, Brookes and Messenger, forwards. kfuddersfleld : Morritt, back ; Kitchen. Deere, Halliwell and Wimpsmny, three quirters ; Sullivan and Dewhurit, halves ; Chambers. Naylor, Knight, Banfrith, Dawson, Driver. Sutcliffe, and Littlewood, forwards, Runcorn won the toss, and commenced hostilities with a vigorous attack, getting quickly to work on the visitors line. where Wilkinsm succeeded in getting over, being brought bac., however for some infringement. By smart play the visitors' custodian relieved matters at a critical moment. A round of passing initiatA by Wicapeunv took the leather out ,of danger. Scrummaging ensued, the IsOme backs gaining possession, Butterworth failing to hold A moment later Faulkner paved splendidly to the same player who failed to tike a rather difficu't pass, a good opportunity being lost. Runcorn were penalized which, for .a moment gave the visitors the upper hand* Lightfoot and Walker changed the venue chargingdheir man with the Dail in his possession and grassing him la fine style, Runcorn were now well within Hu idersfield 25 and some pretty attempts to pierce the defence were seen. From a pack before the goal. Williams managed to get the ball and taking his opponents by surprise sheered through theta and touehed down between the posts. Farmer easily put the leather ' over the cross but. Ruacorn still kept up the pressure re- , peated scrummages taking place on the visitors line. Fine defensive work averted further disaster. A burst away by the visiting front rank 'gave Houghton a chance to di.play his d.fensive powers. Faulkner made a brilliant run which (deserved suzc ells, Tall kicking afterwards ensued leaving Runcorn the advantage. Wirnpenny at this point, shone conspicuously making a capital sprint and beating his man. Houghton, however, was once more reliable and again got his kick in at the right moment. Huddersfield mainly by the efforts of the same player, made r.peated spasmodic eff srts to score but the defence was keen and sure For the first time in the game the Ruaeorn backs were showing somsthing like combination but their final exchanges latices' finish. Several times they should have scored but over-eagerness spoiled their efforts. Half time arrived with Runcorn leading by one goal one try to Huddersfield nil. Changing ends Runecrn kept up the attack. A rush by the visitors made matters warm for Hought da who however, got his kick in splendidly, afterwards collaring his man and throwing him into t inets. A dribble made things look dangerous for the home side but Houghton was again a stumbling block. A fine passing movement by Butterworth and Jones carried the leather the length ot the field. Morrii,t however, proving equal to the emergency. Runcorn were not to be denied and after an exciting burst Warder dropped a fine goal. The visitors after this reverse played U 9 with a little more spirit but the h .me contingent pressed strongly Butterworth ge-ting over only to be brought bick, A series of scrummages took place In which the visitors got the ball repeatedly. Good defensive play frustrated their efforts. The game so the finish was ono of a ding doug character both ends being visited in turn. Final : ituncorn, two goals, one try ; Huddersfield nil.

div.head: SWINTON V. HITNBLET.
div.p: SWINTON V. HITNBLET.

Swintod made their first appearance on the Hamlet ground in the pre,eace of about 13,000 spectetors. Both clubs were well represented. Valentine kicked off for Swinton, and for a long time the game was fought out very close to the Hunslet line. linable% however, forced their way to the Swinton quarter, where A Goldthorpe drop fsd a goal, whilst Lunn shortly afterwards scored a try, which A Goldthorpe improved. liampson scored a try for Swinton, and at half-time Munslet led by seven points to three. On resuming Hunslet commenced to attack vigorously. and for a long time Swinton were kept well inside their own quarter. Hannah made a fine run, and appeared a certain scorer when Lewis tackled him, but in doing so Lewis received an injury which forced him to leave the field. and Barnett filled the vacancy. Hunslet continued to attack, and A Goldthorpe placed a penalty goal. A Goldthorpe dropped another goal Lir Hunslet, and the game ended i Hunslet. four goale and one try (11 points) ; Swinton, one try 'three points).

div.head: BROUGHTON RINGERS v. LEIGH.
div.p: BROUGHTON RINGERS v. LEIGH.

These teams met on the hangers' geourad,befOre about 5,033 spectators. Both clubs were represented, and a splen- didly contested game was played. So evenly matched were the teams and so rapid Wall the rate of scoring that the inter- est in the result of the game was fully maintained to the last moment. Leigh, who were the more powerful set of players. forced matters at the beginning, and played the kick and rash style, which for a time completely baffled the Rangers. They, however, retaliated with passing and com- bination, The game ended :—Broughton Rangers, two goals and three tries (13 points) ; Leigh, two goals end two tries (10 points).
SALFORD V, BATLEY.

Griffiths ommenced th 3 game for Salford. who quickly forced Batley to defend ; but a penalty kick brought relief, and for a short time the game was fought out in midfield. By shirt stsges Batley worked their way to the Salford quarter, where Oakland passed the ball to Spurr, who scored a try. T Williams scored a try for Salford, and at halftime each side had three points ta Its credit. After ends bad been changed Batley were quickly on the attack and from a pass by Oakland Frozzard scored an unimproved try. This was followed by some smart work on the part of Lomas. He pickei up the ball from a scrummase, dodged the Batley hicks, and scored a try for Salford, which he improved. Then Batley appeared to tire, and both Price and T Williams scored tries for Salford. neither of which were converted. In the later stages of the game Auty made a splendid effort to score, but Smith brought hirn down when close to the Salford line. Final score : Salford. one goal and four tries (14 points) ; Batley, two tries (six points). HALIFAX V. BRADFORD. Ten thousanfflpeople gathered at Halifax and a lot of scoring was witnessed. Result :—Bradford four goals and five tries (23 points); Halifax, one goal and two tries (eight points).

_ Fletcher Russell's jturneyei to Swinton on Saturday. Swinton at once pressed, and tries were scored in quick succession by Cooper and George Jones, one of these being improved upon by Valentine. The combination of Flet,her's was poor, but their kicking stood them in goo i stead. Iwo goals were landed by the visitors' custodian from marks neat mid-field. At half-time Swinton were seven pouts ahead. The home team retained the upper hand and .tt Valentine, Jones, Cooper, Williams, and 'Freston were instrumental in increasing the score very materially. The one-sided character of the game continued, and scoring by Swinton became monotonous. The visitors were out.classed, but in spite of this played gamely, their full-back tackling well. div.p: SOUTH EAST LANCASHiRE COM- PETITION.
ROCHDALE HORNETS_ V OLDHAM.

Played at Rochdale, before B.GOO spectators. The visitors were the first to attack, but from a loose dribble the Hornets were dangerous. S Leach scored cleverly at the corner,and Grindroi placed a goal from the touch line, The Hornets pressed hard, and Olderahaw scored a try, Grindrod again placing a goal Half-time score :—Rochdale Hornets, two goals and two tries (ten points) ; Oldham, nil. Soon after resuming Huzzay made a run and scored at the corner, the same player failing at goal. The Oldham men were playing a much better game this half, and Civil scored after good passing, but Huzzey failed at the place kick. The Oldham men played finely, but the Hornets defended well, and pre- vented further snore. Result :—Rochdale Hornets, two goals and two tries (ten points) ; Oldham, two tries (six points).

div.head: Northern Rugby Union Meeting of General Committee.
div.p: Northern Rugby Union Meeting of General Committee.

A meeting of the General Committee of the Northern Union was held at the Spread Eagle Hotel, Manches- ter, on Tuesday evening, Mr J El Houghton (the presi- dent) presiding. The case of Hunslet and Walsh of Birkenhead, was again undsr[consideration, and as the club was found guilty of a breech of the professional laws, it follows that they will have twi points deducted from their score at the next meeting of the Northern Leaeue.

In connection with the case of Mort and the Oldham' L'lub,the prayer was suspended t 3 the end of April, 1903, and Oldham tined £lO. Toe Committeeifound that the Hunslet Club and Walsh had committed & breach of Professional Law 2, and d .cided that the club be fined ono guinea, and Walsh was reinstated from date. The following ruling was asked for by the Yorkshire ?Society of Referees :—" A scrummage is formed, say. ' one yard from goal, and part of the defending forwards in the formation of the pack are actually over the goal 1 ne. Under th 3 sircumscances, is a referee justified in ordering the scrummage further in the Raid of play in order that the pack may be clear of goal lines ? Answer :—Yes. The following suspensions were made :-9 Thomas (Widnes " A "), for striking an opponent. suspended till November 9 ; K Jagger (Eleb- 'den Bridge), for fighting, till November 16 ; W IlEddison (Hunslet), for fighting, till November 16 ; Hall " (Batley), for foul charging, till November 9 ; Thomas (Fletcher Russell), for fighting, till November 16 - Higgins (Runcorn), for kicking an opponent, till Novem: ber 23; winskill (Broughton), for foul charging, two weeks ; J Davies (Birkenhead), for foul charging, one week. Northern League. A meeting of the Northern League was held at the preal E zle Hotel, Manchester, on Tuesday evening, Mr S Gresty presiding. The following were struck off the various recistera Broughton R ingers. R Duck. Warrington, T Traynor, Runcorn, W Sutton. The Stockport Club were fined 30a for late start at Rechdale on October sth, while, for a like o'Zence at Runcorn on the earns day, Hunslet were also ordered to pay 30s. Wins:rill of Broughton Rangers, in the match with Huddersfield, received suspension for a fortnight, the offence being a foul charge. A more seri- ous case was that :a which B Smales, of Bradford, was reported for kicking an opponent in the match at Sal- ford. As the players in question had been sent off the rid, the committee decided taat th is was sufficient punishment for the offence. ,
