div.head: SUICIDE AT THE VULCAN.
div.p: SUICIDE AT THE VULCAN.

On Sunday night a man named Donald Mclntyre of 8, :Manchester-row, Vulcan Vill age, employed as a boiler maker, at the Vulcan Foundry, Earlestown, com- mitted suicide by cutting his throat with .a razor. It appeared that the deceased,who resided with his brother- in-law, Mr llam Wright,had been drinking heavily dur- ing the past fortnight, and had bseri attended by Dr Mouncev for some ailment. On Sunday night Mr. Wright got up and went downstairs ta look for him, when he,was horrified to find him sitting on a chair in the kitchen wt n his throat cut from ear ta ear,and a razlr covered with blood lying on the table. Dr Mnuncey was sent for, but on arrival be found life extinct. Some three months ago the deceased jumped into the river tram the landing stage but was rescued.
THE INQUEST. An inquiry into the circumstacc‘‘s was hold at the Wararave Inn, on Monday evening by Mr 8 Brighouse coroner.

Mr Allll Wright, brother-lc-law of the deceased, was the only witness called and he deposed that the deceased had been living with him for some timP. He was 33 years of age. For the last fortnight he had been drink- ing and bad been under the ca.re of Dr Mouncey. ceased retired to bed with witness on Sunday night at ' half past ten o'clock. Shortly before midnight deceased got up and went downstairs. A few minutes after- wards witness followed and on going into the kitchen found deceased in a chair with his throat cur. The sane with which be had committed the rash, act was on a table in front of him. It had been kept on a high shelf in the kitchen and the deceased must have had it in his possession some time previously because witness and his son were down directly after the deceased left the room. Three months ago deceased attempted to commit suicide by jumping into the river at Liverpool. The magistrates discharged him and allowed witness to take him hcme.
The Coroner : What has been his trouble, drink ? Witness : I cannot tell. It might have been drink. . _

A juror said when he was discharged fer attempted suicide in the Mersey he must have then been considered mentally wrong and ought to have been looked after on that account. He thought it was a grave mistake not to have excercised proper care over him. He should have beers well locked after and not left to himself. Witness said the man was always quiet. - Toe Coroner said ttey did not seem to appreciate the true facts of the case. There was a man who was not quite bad enough to be taken over by the relieving officer and sent to the asylum and his friends felt under an obligation to look after him. Really he could not see that there was, any blame to b 3 attached to his brother-in-law.
A verdict of " Suicide whilst temporarily insane " was returned.

The Coroner said be did not think be would be doing his duty unless he paid a compliment to the police for the ab'e way in which the circumstances of thecase bad been rep.rted to him. Toe man committed suicide at twelve o'clock and at three o'clock iniormation was re- ceivrel at the Ormskirk Police Station. The case came under his notice at seven o'clock when be was arrang- ing his walk for the day and he was enabled to send a message and come there that mght. He thought a very good example had been set by the pOlice,and he thanked them for the expedition they had shown. Sergeant Lines thanked the Coroner for his recognition of their services. It was not often that the police were praised. The brother-in-law of the deceased was then called in, and addressing him, the Coroner slid that the jury and himself attached no blame to him for the unfortunate occurrence. The questions that had been put to him had been put with a view to exonerate him from blame. They understood that he was placed under a heavy re - aronsibility and that he did the best he Could under the circumstances.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. There was an average attendance at the meeting of the P.S.A. Society on Sunday evening. The chair was oc- cupied byMr. William Beswick and the speaker was Mr. Bathgate, of Cressington. In the absence of a soloist, Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus Bac contributed an organ solo with his accustomed ability. The service was also taken part in by the President (Rev. John Yonge), and Messrs D. Owen and Ashton.

Bold-street Wesley Guild. Mr J C Holland presided at the mouthy guild which was held on Monday night. The proceedings consisted of a short address by the Chairman, on the social ad- vantages of the guild as a branch of Church work in which he called attention to the benefits derived from the friendships formed in connection with associations of this kind. After tins a solo was rendered by Mrs J F Prince, and the guild pledges were read over. Mr *right gave a paper on "Reverence," pointing out the various causes which detract from the reverence of public worship. The paper provoked considerable dis- cussion, which was taken part in by Miss Walton, Messrs Holland, Littler, Peake, F Nelson, and H R Sutton, to whom Mr Wright suitably replied. The meet- ing was closed with several short prayers by the members.

Foreign Missionary Anniversary at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. The foreign missionary anniversary services were held in this place of worship on Sunday, when the preacher was the Rev. Henry Haigh, of India. There were good congregations and Mr. Haigh's eloquent dis- courses were listened to with deep interest. A young people's service was held in the afternoon, Mr. James Povey presiding, and an address was delivered by Mr. Haigh. The annual missionary meeting was held in the church on Monday evening. The Rev. Richard Hambley of Lytham presided and there were also present the Revs. Henry Haigh (India deputation), C H. Hocken, T Bishop and J Your and Mr. Pitchford. Mr. Pitchford (secretary, stated in the course of a short report that the amount collected during the year by the juveniles of the Blake system was £7 lls. 7d. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. C. H. Hocken submitted a general report. He stated that this circuit had contributed to the Foreign Missionary Society during the year 1903 £232, being an increase on the preceding year of 1 £32 is. 4d. Towardo that amount Bewsey-road had contributed £3B 4s. ad. He went on to say that the Missionary Society was never more in need of their prayerful sympathy and generous support than now. On the one hand the income was collected when the twentieth century fund, the war funds and the Indian famine fund were also appealing to the generosity of their people. On the other hand the urgent appeals for increased help from every part of the mission field 'were never more urgent than now. He need only mention the piteous appeals from their West Indian churches plunged in poverty by appalling commercial disasters. They thought of the unlimited openings for aggressive work on the West Coast of Africa. They ccu'd not forget the Transvaal where on account of the war their missionaries had been compelled to leave the country ; thousands of their native converts had been scattered ; and their churches closed. They thought of India where their native churches had been impoverished by famine and decimated by plague. And they had multitudes of destitute children from among their own people and from the famine camps appealing to them foe Christian charity. Then their eyes turned to the farther East and they thought of China, where through the geographical position of their mission districts no lives had ,been lost yet in consequence of the recent troubles, the women and children of their missionaries had had to be removed to places of safety and their work bad been suspended. When they thought of all these things they must feel that their missionary society never had greater need of their prayerful and intelligent sympathy and ger3eroii'.v than at present.. At the dawn of this new century they saw opportunities for carry- ing the Gospel to willing hearers unparalleled in the his- tory of the world since the days of Christ,and he thought if he rightly understood the spirit of the people in Bewsey -road they were prepared to do their fair share in sending their missionaries of the cross into all parts of the world that all men might hear 0 The glorious news of sins forgiven, of bell subdued and peace with heaven." The7,Police Court ana Prison Gate Mission. The following are some of the principal statistics of the work of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Liverpool Diocesan Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society for the month of October. The number of police and petty sessional courts visited was twenty-six. During 261 attendances the Missionaries conversed with 1287 persons in the cells and courts of whom 705 were visited in their abodes after the adjournment of the courts. Employment was provided for 12 men and lads, 63 women, girls and boys were taken to homes restored to parents and friends, or provided with work. In two cases the loss of employment was averted by the intercession of missionaries. 90 cases were attended to at the request of the Magistrates. and 61 at the suggestion of the police and the Court officials. In 34 instances clothing was supplied to enable persons to accept work. The Mission room near Walton prison was open every week-day morning when the prisoners were being discharged of whom 679 were provided with breakfast, and were given advice. employment, &c. 33 tickets were given to men for work at the Society's Firewood and Mat Factory, Bootle, The Women's Temperance Home received two addi- tional inmates. The names and addresses of 18 persons were sent to the Clergy and Ministers of religion for visitation, 258 total abstinence pledges administered, 80 meetings were addressed, &c., &c

div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS. No man has so many offers of assistance as the man who needs none.

THE GREAT POlNT.—Biggs: "Where is your family going to spend the summer ?" Miggs : " don't know yet. My wife hasn't found out which place is most expens.ve." NOT EXPLICIT.—" Sir," said the stranger, "1 am an artist." "So?" queried the other, "What sort? Rszor, fiddle, brush, pugilistic, or stage r MEMORIES OF THE Micraoroms.—The Squire : "So you've got back from London. How did you feel in such a big city ?" Father Sturnpley " felt for my purse most o' th' time, surr." "How savagely that cow looked at me." "It'd your red hat my dear." "Well ! I knew it was a little out of fashion, but I didn't suppose a country cow would notice it." "NEVER write letters, young man, that regret in after-life." "You speak as from ex. perience." "I do ! In early correspondence with her who is now my wife I signed myself, Your obedient servant.'" "I'm making money by selling mice." "Whom do you sell them to?" "The professor of music it the next street." "What on earth does ha want mice for?" "Why, he uses them for trying the voices of the young ladies." "CAN you change a £5 note for me?" he asked, with an important air that nettled the courteous clerk. "Yes, sir; we can change anything here." "Wish you'd change my mind, then, if you're sc good at it." "Have no small change, sir." "Mn. Ilottris is a splendid fellow, I think," said Miss Perkins. "Yes," said Ethel ; "but he is very absent-minded. When we were first en- gaged he used to call me Alice—he said that was his mother's name, which was also forgetful, because I've found out since it was Mary." "Get out of my way !" angrily shouted the man with the diamond scarf pin. "You're half-seas over !" " Yes, I'm half-seas over," replied the webbing pedestrian, "but I'll be all right to-mor- row. But there's no hope for you. Every morn. ing you will get up the same sort of a vagabond.,' THEIR AUNT: "And so you're going to buy your uncle a pipe with your pennies instead ol spending them on chocolate?" The Dear Children: " Yes ; then uncle will give us a shilling, and we can spend that on sweets." THE PHILOSOPHER "A young man should begin at the bottom and work his way up." The Youth : "I can't very well do that. lam appren- ticed to a well-digger." MR. GUSHER : "So you're spending Christmas with your married sister, I presume, Miss Prinker ? Did you come down by the mail train, last night ?' Miss Prinker (blushing modestly): "Well, yes—. I did. But—but—but—in a ladies' carriage." A NEW clergyman was taking Sunday duty in a hamlet among the Yorkshire Wolds. After morn- ing service the clerk came up to him, and observed : "So ye call them 'Sauums, do ye? Noo, we never knew what to make o' that ere 'P.' We silos called 'em 'Spasms.'" MRS. WICKWIRE. : "What ridiculous, impossible things these fashion plates are." Mr. Wickwire: "I know they used to be, but most of them are engraved from photographs nowadays." Mrs. Wickwire: " This one can't be. Here are two woman going in opposite directions, both with brand new gowns on, and neither looking back at the other." "HAVEN'! you and your friend finished with that argument yet?" "It isn't my argument," answered tho opinionated man resentfully. "I sin merely telling him the facts in the case, and he is so thick he can't understand." WIFE: "You mustn't worry so much dear; it will make you ill." Husband : " Not ill, but cross-eyed." Wife: " Cross-eyed ?" Hushand : " Yes ; trying to look at my income and my ex- penses at the same time." TEACHER : "If any pupil can answer, let her raise her hand. Well, Mary, you may tell." "Please, ma'am, I don't know." "Then why did you raise your hand?" "I couldn't help it, ma'am. Uncle John gave me this bangle last night." OLD LADY (on ocean steamer): "Mercy me! Is this all one ship?" Travelled Grand-daughter : "Why, yea, grandma, and we haven't walked a quarter the length of it yet." " Gracious : How near will we be to America when we get to the other end?" "MY husband,' says the large lady, "has a habit of marking all paragraphs in the paper that say mean things about women." "So that you will not fail to seem them, ela 7 Still, that is not as mean a trick as mine plays. He cuts them all out. Then I have to get another paper, only to find that I have been made a silly of." A GOOD Su.—Mrs. Newwed: "I can't under- stand it, mamma, but Harry is an altogether different man since we were married." Mamma : "My dear child, I should be alarmad if he were not. A man who remained the same after mar- riage as he was daring courtship would be an anomaly. Really, I should fear there was some- thing wrong in his intellect."

N—EWSBOY—: "Paper, sir?" City Man: "What papers have you?" Newsboy: "Look here, mister, I've got ter work for my livin'. I know th' names of all th' pnpers I carry, but I ain't got no time to stand here and recite'em. Come round some Sunday afternoon." PAPA: "You saw that big boy whipping the little one, and you didn't interfere? Suppose you had been that little boy?" Bobbie: "I did think of that, an' was going to part 'ern, but then I hap. to think, s'pose I was the big boy? So I left 'ain alone." "I'm sorry about this war in South Africa." "It doesn't affect you personally." " Yes it does. Half-a.dozen girls have told me it was going to make diamonds more expensive. P'raps it was my egotistic imagination: but every one of them seemed to have a now-is-the.tiine-to-buy.engage. ment-rings' look in her eye." COCKNEY (to Rural Stationmaster): "What's on at the theatre, tonight!" Rural Stationmaster: "Theayter ! Why, we ain't got acy, sir." Cockney: "Oh I Anybody particular at the masic•hall, then?" Rural Stationmaster: " Moo- sik 'all! There ain't any ; but there's shunting every night on the branch line, and everybody comes up to see that." GRANDMA bad been explaining to the little girl how our earth is kept from flying off into infinite space by the attraction of the sun, which is con. satantly trying to draw the earth towards ltaelf, while the latter always keeps its distance. " Grand- mamma," said the little girl, "I should think the sun would get discouraged after a while and let go." ANNETTE: "I have just been having a delight- ful stroll with Harold. Can anything ba me:o poetical than a walk in the moonlight?" Jean- nette (five years older): "Poetical, no doubt, Annette: but when you have had my experience you will know that a dark corner of the stairs is equal to ten moonlight nights." FOR Two REASONS.—"I would go with you to the end of the earth," he asserted passionately. "Not with me you wouldn't," she replied coldly. " Wny not ?" he demanded. "For two reasons," she answered. "One is that I'm not going, and the other is that there isn't any end." When one meets the prosaic New Woman one has to be care- ful what he says. A FARMER once sent half-a-crown for a lightning caterpillar-killer, which he saw advertised in 3 paper, and received by return two blocks of wood, with directions printed on theta as follows: "Take this block, which is No. 1, in the right hand; place the caterpillar on No. 2, and press them together. Remove the caterpillar, and pro- ceed as before." "HAS George ever hinted that he had thought of you as a possible wife?" asked the anxious mother. "No," replied the girl, a far-away look In her eyes, "and I'm afraid he never will." " Why," said the mother, "I thought—" "It doesn't matter what you thought, mamma, dear," interrupted the daughter. "Only last night he complained of feeling drowsy, and it wasn't nine o'clock. A Lawns was cross-examining a bad-tempered woman, who was evidently a mateh for any man, whilst her husband, who was obviously the weaker vessel, sat eheepiehly listening. The lawyer was pressing a question urgently, when she said, with fire flashing from her eyes: "You needn't try to' catch me, sir; you tried that once before 1" "Madam," replied the counsel, "I haven't the slightest desire to catch you, and your husband looks as if he was sorry he did."

div.head: Municipal Trading, Etc.
div.p: Municipal Trading, Etc.

Sir,—l attended the meeting at Parr Hall on Wednes• day, when the campaign of insult and calumny which has been conducted against the Corporatim for so many months entered upon a new phase. 1 Persistent misrepresentation has not been entirely without effect, and it would appear that a considerable number of honest, but not very well informed persons have come to think that the charges of corruption against the Council and its officials are well founded. It was with regret that I saw gentlemen like Messrs. Dodds, Bindlose, and S. Kenyon lending themselves to this agitation ; they at any rate are of a very different type from those who commenced it, and have dissocia- ted themselves frcm the coarser misrepresentations and malicious personalities of some of their colleagues ; their good faith is above suspicion though they have shown a lamentable willingness to believe evil of men not greatly inferior to them in intelligence and integrity ! and who work in the Council with a single eye for the common good. The attack is being now concentrated on two points : with one of these the consolidation of the debt, the Chairman of the Finance Committee dealt in the Council Chamber on Tuesday evening ; the other is the questisn of Corporation Contracts, on which I should like to offer a few comments. _

Premising that I am by intellectual conviction a Demccrat and a Free Irader, recognising that the faults of our present electoral and governmental methods are that they are neither democratic nor free enough, and rejoicing that slowly but surely the stream of social tendency is bearing us to greater freedom and more complete democracy, I shall always etrenucusly oppose any efforts to restrict the powers of the people's repre- sentatives either by legiclative enactment or by the further subordination of local authorities to departmertt of the Central Government. hero then is the real check upon improper conduct by the Councillors? It is with the electors; and I tor one unhesitatingly main- tain that if there is to be any change in the law it should he in the direction of greater freedom rather than of increased restrairt. If the ratepayers elect honest and competent representatives, if those represen- tatives cmploy honest and competent officials, and if the contracts for labour and material are let by open tender on public advertisement, all the conditions neces- sary for securing efficient public service will have been observed. All these conditions ottain in Warrington ; let anyone who has any evidence to the contrary pro- duce it ; if the cowardly slanderers who have so long indulged in charges of general corruption against the Corporation can bring forward one single definite case ag,ainst any member of it, or aaainst any one of its officials, let it be clearly set forth, Mr Pemberton at leatt had the courage to commenca legal:proceedings,with:decidedly disastrous consequences to himself. Whether anyone else will do so remains to be seen. It has been my fortune to secure the confi- .dence of a large number of my fellow townsmen whose tnt.rests I have striven to serve both as a member of the Board of Guardians, and of the Town Council. I am very jealous of the honour of both these bodies, and am not ashamed to say that I keenly resent the fabrications of native and imported malignity with which the fair fame of our good old town has beenlbeemirched.—Yours faithfully, ALF. J. JOLLEY. 16, Arpler-street, October 31st, 1901.

div.head: Raffling and Roulette at Bazaars.
div.p: Raffling and Roulette at Bazaars.

Sir,—Permit me once more to raise my empriatie protest against the immoral and illegal praetice of gambling in the form of raffles at bazaars which is now being carried to extremes which are simply preposter- ous. If I am correctly imformad this form of gambling

was carried at the recent Roman Catholic Bazaar to the iniquitous length of roulette tables and of raffling for champagne, whisky, and even five pound notes. No wonder the witness for social and national righteous- ness is so feeble in our variously organised religious systems whose standard of " holiness of life " is apparently as low as their appreciation of the forces of evil against which they are—Heaven save the mark !—supposed to be arrayed. The higher conscience of the community to which these systems, if they are to be of any saving use, should address themselves is outraged, and in many cases completely alienated. On all sides we hear of the alarming growth of the gambling spirit. And can we be surprised when so far from effectively rebuking it our religious communities—yes I include my own—too often ostentatiously encourage and bless it? Gambling is generally only condemned because of the ruin and misery it so often entails. It is not thought wrong in itself. And raffling is too often regarded as a practice perfectly innocent It is compared with drink- excess in drink is condemned; excess in gamb- ling is also condemed. But it is argued that just as there is nothing wrong in the moderate use of alcohol so there is nothing wrong in the moderate indulgence in gambling such as obtains at bazaars. The comparison, however, is absurd, the argument fallacious. For wherein lies the sin of intoxication. Is it not in the suspension of the control of reason in the one intoxi- cated ? And to transfer property by chance—as is done in a raffle—is to deny the control of reason in the act, just as intoxication is the suspension of reason in all acts. Both are alike, if not to the same extent, immoral. In all legitimate transactions the duty of reason is to reduce chance to a minimum. But in gambling chance is made the chief if not the sole deter- mining principle. The wrong of gambling therefore consists not in its excessive indulgence—this intensifies and complicates the wrong—but in surrendering to mere chance actions which reason should control in accordance with moral law. It has been said with truth that "a man's first bet is like his first bout." He in both instances has denied reason and ignored the moral law which should influence and determine his action inreference to his brother man. Gambling is thus seen to be wrong in itself—however small the effects of that wrong may appear in anyone particular raffle, just as intoxication is wrong in itself,however small the effects of that wrong may appear in any one particular bout. But when we know from judges, magistrates, and head-constables, as well as from clergy, and other ministers of religion how disastrous are the ravages which gambling and ' betting—like intoxication—are causing in our midst, is it too much to ask the former to carry out the law of which they are the administrators not only with regard to the bookmakers at the street corners but also with regard to the promoters and supporters of raffles at our " religious" bazaars—and the latter—our ministers of religion—to abstain from every kind, form, or appear- ance (however they translate S. Paul's Greek in I Thess. Sc. 22) of evil which brings so unsettling, degrading, hardening, avaricious and other pernicious conse- quences in its train. Yours &c., FRANCIS E. POWELL. I St. James' Vicarago, Latchford, October 31st, 1901.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DIS- TRICT COUNCIL.
Resignation of the Gas and Water
Engineer.

The monthly meeting of the Urban District Council was held at the Town Hall, Earlestown on Monday evening. Mr W Collingwood presided and there were also present Messrs C B F Borron, E T Evano, T Ormand. J W Emmett, W Gilmour, Dr-Latham. N iddcley, J Simpson, with C Cole (clerk), A B 3wes (surveyor) and H U Timmins (gas and water engineer). THE INADEQUATE LIGHTING OF THE MAIN

div.head: STREETS.
div.p: STREETS.

_ The engineer submitted his report as to the lighting of streets in the district, in which he stated that in some instances it might bp necessary Ito alter the position of existing lamps. Be suggested the fixing of one addi- tional lamp in each of the following streets :—Queen- street, Brookfield-street, King-street, Lord-street, St John-street (new property), Heald-street, Wharf-road (bend), Fairclougt-street, Sankey-street, Nelson-street (new property), Regent-street, Rydal-street, Wargrave; two additional lamps in Bank-street and in the road leading from Earls-street to Variel-square ; three addi- tional lamps in Brick-street (continuation of Regent- street) and four additional lamps in Haydock-street, It was resolved that the recommendations of the engineer be carried cut as soon as possible; also that the engineer be directed to prepare and submit to the next meeting of this committee a report as to the lighting of public footpaths and of other places requiring light in the dis- trict. Mr Thompson moved the confirmation of the minutes,

Mr. Ormand referred to the minute relating to the lighting of st.eets and said that two very important streets had been omitted—Bridge-street, and Market- stree. Market-itreet particularly, was very badly lighted and to a very large extent the tradespeople loa‘d to be depended upon for the lighting of that thorough- fare. After the business premises were closed the street was inadequately lighted. The same remark applied, to a lesser extent to Bridge-street. Mr. Simpson said that Mil!-lane was very badly lighted and he suggested that tt.o engineer should be requested to report upon the matter. Mr. Gilmour said that the Council had agreed that incandescent lights should be fixed opposite places of worship, and there was a lamp opp,xi:e the Mission hall in Brunswick-3treet which had not an incandescent burner. Lie recommended that this lamp be placed on the list.

The Clerk said he had rezeived an application from Mr. Drina for an incandescsnt light opposite the mission hall and he had replied stating that the matter would be p'a,:ed before the Gas Committee. Mr Ormand moved that Bridge-street, Market-street and Mill-lane be added to the list mentioned.

Dr Latham objected to the matter being brought directly before the Council meeting without being men- tioned in committee. If they were going to have in- candescent lights in Mil!-lane they aught to have them all over the place. Mr Thompson referring to Mr Ormand's motion said the streets in question were reported upon by the en- gineer, and would it not meet the wishes of Mr Ormand if the engineer prepared a report upon the other streets and presented it at the next meeting of the committee. Mr. Ormand said that unfortunately be was unable to attend the Committee meeting, or he should cei taiuly not have brought the matter forward at the Council meeting. The engineer was requested to prepare a report, and the report v. as submitted. He considered the streets be had referred to were an omission, and he asked that the omissionlbe remedied, Mr Ormand's resolution was not seconded, and the mlnutas were approved: Th 3 lighting question will be brought forward at the next committee meeting. WATER COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended that the tender of Messrs Richard Evans and Company, Limited, for the supply of slack to the Water Works during the period encing the 30th June,el9o2, be accepted. It was resolved that the report of the Special Water Sot-Com- mittee be approved and adopted, and that Messrs. Read and Waring, engineers, of Westminster, London, be engaged to undertake to make a careful examination of the proposed scheme to prepare preliminary plans and estimates for the Local Government Board Inquiry and attend such inquiry, and on approval of the scheme to make all necessary working drawings and prepare specifications of the various works to be carried out, examine and report on the tenders, and to superintend the work at manufacturers and during constructioc;and tnat the remuneration to be paid to them be that set forth in the recommendation of the sub-committee. The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr Barron seconded by Mr Gi:mnur. HIGHWAYS AND SANITARY COMIIITTEE. A SATISFACTORY HEALTH REPORT. CONDITION .OF SANKEY BROOK. At a meeting of the Highways and Sanitary Commit- tee, the following building plans were approved and passcd :—Eli Bunting, seven dwelling-houses, Nevidc- street (subject to manhole being provided) •,William Monks (33, Tamworth-street) and George Randall (126, Legh-street), two dwelling-houses, Haydock-street.— The following building plans were disapproved Walker and and Shepherd (Yew Tree Farm), twenty loose boxes for [horses, Newton Racecourse ; The Northern I Investment Co., (Crust-lane, Earlestnwn), twenty-eight houses, stables and yard, School-street, Patterson-street, and Foundry-street.-4 letter was read from the Sur- veyor to the Warrington Rural District Council stating that the Vulcan Foundry, Ltd., had made application to that Council to make arrangements for the recon- struction of Alder Root Lane Bridge, that the Vulcan Foundry, Ltd., were willing to hear half of the cost, that the Warrington Rural District Council were of opinion that it would be unfair to ask them to do even so :much as it would be of little benefit to that district without the road on the Earlestown side of the brook being formally taken over, dedicated to the putlic, and put into thorough condition, and that los was directed ,to obtain the views of this Council thereon. It was I resolved that the Surveyor be directed to report to the next meeting or the Committee with respect thereto.

The Medial Officer of Health read his quarterly ' re- port, from which it appeared tbat during the quarter ending September 30. h, there were registered : Births, 53 males, 68 females. total 121 ; deaths, 30 males, 31 females, total 61. The excess of births over deaths was 60. The birth-rate was 30 4 and the death- rate 14.5 per 1,000 of the estimated population. The cases notified under the Infectious Disease (Notifination) Act, 1889, were 56 in number or 3.3 per 1,000 for the quarter, Sixteen cases were removed to the Isolation Hospital. The dector continues :—I alll convinced there would have been fewer cases of scarlet fever had the accommoda, ion requ,sitioned by us been conceded, We observe the weekly publication of cases in the Hospital, and cannot see the reason for the sus- pension of the admission of our cases when there is, apparently at least, room for them. It was resolved that the Clerk be instructed to write to the vVarriegton Isolation Hospital Authorities with respect to the sus- pension of the admission of patients from this District. The surveyor presented a report with respect to the Water Ca triage System, and said that he considered that while the present system was one which was fairly satisfactory from a sanitary point of view, it might be advisable to adopt a Water Carriage System on the grounds of economy, and the waste water system would be more suitable for this district than would ordinary water closets. It was reselved that a clause he inserted in the proposed new bye-laws, requiring that new pro- perty be provided with water closets. The surveyor re- ported that he had made an inspection of Sankey Brook from the boundary of this district as far as St Helens, with a view to finding out the sources of pollution. Ha found at one point a stream known as the Black Brook -flowing into Sankey Brook from Haydock, and appar- ently containing sewage. On the boundaries of Parr he found a large sewer discharging into an open channel of brickwork. There was a very large body of inky-black sewage flowing down at the rate lof many hundreds of thousands of gallons per elay into Sankey Brock. There is some slight pollution from a few cottages in the Burtonwood district, and also from the Havanna aod Sauthport Collieries. It was resolved that the surveyor he directed to communicate with the surveyor to the Warrington Rural District Council on the subject. The committee recommended that the application of the Industrial Co-operative Society for a slauenter-house licence for their premises in Suez-street be granted for a period of twelve months from the 29% September last. The Cbairman moved, and Mr Simpson seconded the cenfirthation of the minutes. _

Mr Rorron said he thought the Council ought to note very carefully the satisfactory report of the Medical Officer of Health. He found that the average of the death rate in the Newton district was 14.5, whilst the general average of the County for urban districts was 174. In the neighbouring district of Haydock, for the three months ending S3ptember 30%, the death rate was 28 2, whilst at Ashton it was 25, and at Golborns 18.2. Ile trusted that when they had the refuse destructor and the isolation hospital erected that the health or the district wouldf continue to improve and be a model to the surrounding districts. (Hear, hear). GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. -7,n.

div.p: BEMJTIFYING TflE TOWN FULL._

At a meeting of the above committee the following report of the sub-committee appointed to consider the Surveyor's suggesions for"the beautifying of the Town Hall, was read and approved, viz. :—(a) The Surveyor's suggestions for the beautifying of the fowl) Hall, which were submitted to the Highways and Sani- tary Committee on the 22nd of July last, and by them referred to this sub-committee were considered. After the sub—committee hid made an inspection of the building, it was resolved that the General Purposes Committee be recommended to carry out the Surveyor's suggestions, including the minor details which the sub- committee suggest should be done. It was also decided to recommend that the hat rail at present in the Board room be removed therefrom and placed in the cloak room, and to call the committee's attention to the state of the Board roem carpet. A letter was read from the Clerk of the Peace for the County stating that he would submit to the Standing Joint Committee, at their nest meeting, draft bye-laws to prohiti: betting in

street?. It was resolved that the Council be recommended to make application to the County Standing Joint Committee for an increase in the number of police for the district, the present staff being considered inadequate. The minutes were approved. RESIGNATION OF THE GAS AND WATER ENGINEER.

At a meeting of the—gSS-ff—Co—m-M-ittee s letter was read from mr:a o Timmins, resigning his position as gas and water engineer to the Council, the resignation to take effect on January 31st. It was resolved that the Council be recommended to accept such resignation. It was also resolved that the Clerk be instructed to ad- vertise for a mill-wright, having experience of pumping engines and water-works plant aact also of general work and that hi be paid a wage at the rate of £l2O per annum. It was resolved that a water and gas engineer be engaged at a commencing salary of £3OO per annum and that the engineer be appointed to act as clerk to the works during the carrying out of the waterworks scheme.

Mr. Ormand moved and Mr. Siddeley seconded the adoption of the minutes. Mr. E. T. Evans moved that the matter be deferred until the next meeting. The subject was a most im- portant one and he should like all the members of the Council to be present and vote upon it. There was no seconder to the amendment and the minutes were passed. This was all the business of public iaterest.

div.head: Runcorn School] Board Election.
div.p: Runcorn School] Board Election.

Sir,—Seeing that the School Board Election is close at hand, I sincerely hope there will be none of the religious element introduced as was the case at the election three years ago ; not so much of " down with the rates," but a little more information on the Educa- tion question. I would ask is it possible to " down with the rates" which ever side gets in. I think not, as we have to keep finding increased accommodation as the number of children increases and also to provide the most efficient teaching staff. The returns show the School Board teaching staff has been most efficient. We all know that Board Schools are public institutions sup- ported from the rates, therefore why do the candidates who wish to represent us, put themselves into groups and call themselves churchmen and progressives. Rate- payers I say put your foot down, and say your institu- tions shall not be dominated by any sect or creed, bait by gentlemen who have the education question at heart, let them be church or chapel. The moment they are elected to the Board the members ought to be educa- tionalists first and churchmen or chapelmen afterwards Where do we stand tc-day as an educational country ? Fifty years behind either Germany, Italy, Norway or Sweden. Our country and our colonies are literally over run with Germans who fill our counting-houses and our laboratories while the child of a poor English- man is brought up to use a pick and a shovel and little else. And why ? Because of the religious feeling that , is incorporated in our educational system. Now fellow ratepayers this month we shall have the option of saying who shall represent us on:the School Board. Is it not possible to find gentl,men in Runcorn who will come forward as edu- cationists, independent of any denomination, and repre- sent the ratepayers in a true sense by making it pos- sible for a workingman's child who has brains to get the test education possible. Do not on any account allow our public institutions to be monopolised by folowers of any creed. Sectarianism has been the greatest draw- back to education and if sectarians control our School Board,so much the worse for the ratepayers' schools. It was sectarianism that was at the back of the Cockerton judgment which has aimed a dastardly blow at the evening schools where our youths ought to continue their education. I sincerely hope the gworking class population of Runcorn will not be led by any false views such as " down with the rates." If we are to have substantially, built schools, with healthy surroundings, and an efficient teaching staff for our children it is an utter impossibility to " down with the rates." The money is well spent. The Elementary Education Act was really passed for the benefit of the working classes, therefore let us support Board Schools and give our children the education they could never have had hut for the Act which made Board Schools possible. No one will doubt that I am a churchman, nor dare question my Conservatism, but on this question I am for education first, education second, and education third,and my vote will go to that man or that set of men who set education before party or religion.—Yours truly, PETER RADLEY. 12, Eaton-street, Runcorn.

div.head: FATAL FOG.
div.p: THE FATAL FOG.
Sad Drowning Fatality,
A Warrington Young Man Falls into the
Woolston Canal.

An Inquest .was conducted at the "flog and Partridge " Inn,Woolston, on Wednesday afternoon by ML 8 Brighouse, County Coroner, touching the death of George Davies; 21 years of age, a puddler, residing at 49, Allen-street, who was drowned in the Woolston canal at Paddington Lock on Sunday , evening. Evidence of identification having been given by deceased's father. May Sankey said that she and deceased kept company. They left home about 6.15 on Sunday evening to go for a walk. They were crossing the canal at Paddington Locks by means of the pro- jecting plank when deceased missed his footing and tell into the water. Witness screamed and deceased shouted " Help " and assistance came. The body was recovered at about 750. The night was rather foggy. They had often gone that way together, Mary Rathbone said her husband was the lock- keeper at Paddington. On Sunday night they heard a scream and witness ran out. She returned for a light and went back to the locks and saw the deceased sink in the water. A life buoy was thrown to him but he did not get hold of it. John Rathboue, the lock-keeper, said he was some distance away when the scream was heard. He went to the lock and recovered the body. It was a very foggy night. The lock gates were pri- vate property and people had no right to use the , plank by which deceased was crossing. There was a prop•q• way across the canal higher up. A verdict of "Accidental death was returned.

Trap Accident in Winwick-street. A trap accident occurred in Winwick-road at about 10 15 on Sunday night. Two conveyances, one a hansom belonging to John Monk., of Leigh, driven by Henry Briscoe, who resides at 13. Ducie- street, Leightand the other a trap driven by George Hatton, butcher, 42, Boardman-street, Warrington, came into collision near Warburton-street. The man Briscoe fell from the hansomand the shafts of the trap were smashed. P C Dawson came up and found him on the floor unable to walk. He was taken to the Infirmary and attended by Dr Fergu- son, who found that he had been badly shaken and bruised about the legs. He was afterwards taken home.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
The Boer Losses at Bethel.
Lord Kitchener 6tateB that the Boer losses in the fight with C Benson's column were 44 killed and 100 wounded.
Theist South Lancashire Regiment at Vryheid.
Letter from Major Adam.
A Boer Testimonial.
The Mayor of Warrington has received the following letter from Major A lam, in command of the 1c S auth Lancashire Regiment, now at the front. Vryheid, Transvaal. 18th September, 1901, _

Dear Mr Mayor,— Tne warm clothing and other welcome articles which you so kindly sent to this battalion , from the citizens of Warrington came here by the con- voy which reached us on 13:h September, and were unpacked yesterday. To-day we hope to distribute them to all ranks here, and to send back a proportion to 1 MHO 100 odd men who are detached frem us and doing duty at De Jagers Drift and other places on the Buffalo River. I had written you previously to thank you in anticipation, but to hear that your handsome gilt has at last reached us will give satisfaction to all those who so kindly contributed. We received other things from other persons,and I endow a list of the totals of articles received, which may be of seine interest. Some pack- ages always come without any internal or externs 1 evidence of the consignor, but so far as we can we have tried to trace packages to,their source of origin. Though the warm clothing has arrived at the concha- sion of the winter, it will be none the less welcome,,for we are having some very wet and cold weather, and the nights are raw and Way. Men on " Sentry go" are consequently only too glad to have an additional warm garment,and your presents will serve a very use- ful purpose in keeping the sentries warm. Allow me to convey to you, and through you, to all the good people of Warrington,our sincere gratitude for their fresh proof of interest in your own particular line regiment. We are doing our beat to prove a credit to you, although our work is more arduous and anxious at present than brilliant; bat I think I may say that our men have worked so hard at the defences here for some eight months, and keep so vigilant a look-out at night, that the Boers refuse to "take us on." Indeed they are reported to have said "It was no good attacking Vryheid, they were always on the look-out."—The men are very fit and well as a whole.—Believe me to be, dear Mr Mayor, yours bincerely and gratefully, F. A. ADAM, Major, Commanding lit South Lancashire Regiment. His Worship The Mayor of Warrington. P.S.—I could not send this letter to catch last Mail,as there was a big concentration of some 4,000 to 5,000 Boers in Blood River Valley,and on 17th lost they caught Gough's Mounted Infantry in a trap and captured the lot, SOMS 350 in all, killlng some 25, wounding 43 more, and capturing 260. Their treatment of the dead, wounded and prisoners was barbarous, they stripped all alike of boots and clothes. Dead, wounded and prisoners were sent in here, as Botha wrote asking O.C. Vryheid to send out ambulances. You will be glad to know that our men from their presents just received, gave about 150 lbs of tobacco and warm clothing to the prisoners, who were most grateful. I will write more later. Boers had a lot of armed Kaffir fighting for them !—F.A.A. div.head: AN INHUMAN--.FATHER AT FRODSHAM.
div.p: AN INHUMAN--.FATHER AT FRODSHAM.
Tries to tHang his Son.

At the Frodsham Folic Court last Friday, before Messrs Charles Reynolds (in the chair) and Alfred Thomas, a labourer named Thomas Fletcher, of Five Crosses, was charged on a warrant, at the instance ot Inspector Hackett, of the N.S.P.C.C., with haying nee"- tented and Unrested his two children, Richard, aged 12, and Frank, aged two. Mr. Browne, for the Prosecution, said the case had been under Inspector Hackett's supervision since January, 1900, and amendments had from time Co time been made by the defendant, out in consequence of the serioua complaints of the neighbours Inspector Hackett found on Wednesday that the boy Richard was suffer- ing from a black eye the result of a blow from his fattier and on making further inquiries he discovered that the lad was very dirty, and that he had not had his shirt changed for three months and on taking some off it had to be burned and a new one supplied. The man was of drunken habits and was continually thrashing the lad. He made him get up at four o'clock in the morning to light the fire, and cook defendant's breakfast, and then no lad was left to himself all the day long until the public-houses had closed at night when the defendant invariably returned home under the influence of drink. The lad wcighed 10lbs less than the lowest normal weight, and be was so afraid of his father that the police found him in a closet last Tuesday night. Evidence was ttes given by the boy who told the Bench that his father thrashed him almost every night and that he had not tasted butcher's meat for a con- siderable time. He also said that his father attempted to hang him on Sunday night last. The boy's statement was corroborated by three neighbours,all of whom said the house was in* shock- ing condition and the defendant being a widower there had never been any woman in the house since his wife died, defendant having made the boy do the work. Evidence was given by P.C. Fry (wha gave the defen- dant a very bad character with regard to his conduct to his son), and r:1 go by Inspector Hackett, both having repeatedly warned defendant. He was not fit to have the custody of the children. Dafendant said he only thrashed the boy because he could not get him to attend schoc I, and that he had the same food as he (defendatt) had. The Chairman said it was drink that had brought defendant into his present position, and he would have to go to gaol for three calendar months with hard labour. On inquiring what would be done with the children, Mr Browne explained that Inspector Hackett would communicate with the head quarters of the society in London, and in all probability application would be made at the next sessions for the boy Richard to be sent to the ship Clio (be having expressed a wish to go). and that the boy Frank should be given into the Custody of Mrs Warren, a neighbour, who, in the opinion of those in Court, was most attached to him.

div.head: WATER SUPPLY OF NEWTON DISTRICT. __-- Local Government Board Inquiry.
div.p: THE WATER SUPPLY OF NEWTON DISTRICT. __-- Local Government Board Inquiry.

Colonel W. Langton Coke, M. Jest,, C.E., an Inspec- tor cf the Local Government Board, conducted an inquiry in the town Hall, Earlestown, on Wednesday morning, into the application of the Urban District Council of Newton-in-Makerfi 1d for sanction to borrow £20,700 for purposes of their water undeitaking. There were present : Mr J W Collingwood (chairman), bar C B F Borron (chairman of the Water Committee), Dr Patterson, Dr Latham, Dr Watkins (medical officer of health), Mr T Ormand, Mr Wood, Mr Thompson, with Mr Colo (clerk), Mr Bowes (surveyor), sod Messrs Read and Waring (consulting water engineers of Westminster, London).
STATEMENT BY THE CLERK.

At the outset Mr. Cole male the following statement to the Inspector respecting the application :—The application which was made to the Local Government Board in September last was to sanction the borrowing by the Council of the sum of £20,700 to carry out the following works for completing the Council's Scheme for the provision of a proper supply of water to the inhabit- ants of their district, viz. :—Section 11. Well lift, by 6lt. 20011. deep, £1,200 ; 600 feet cunnelling, £1:500 ; duplicate pumping engine, £1,390 ; engine house, addi- tional size, £3OO ; travelling crane. £l4O ; cottage, £4OO ; contingencies, £570 ;—£6,000. Section 111. Service reservoir (to hold about 500,000 gallons ef water), £4,700 ; elevated tank, £1,600 ; cottage, £4OO ; —£6,700. New distribution mains, £3,000. Total, £20,700. These estimates were prepared by the late Engineer to the Council. The Council, having recently gone fully into the question of the appointment of engineers to superintend the carrying out of the proposed works. appointed Messrs Read and Waring, of Westminster, as toeir engineers for this work. I may here mention that the Council took this step with the view of obtaining the best possible advice ou their undertaking. Messrs Read and Waring have carefully examined the proposed scheme and have revised the estimates of tho cost of laying new distribution mains. They estimate that a sum of £9,700 is req aired for that purpose instead of £3,000 as inserted in the original estimate. This increase is caused by an error in estimating the length of pipes required to be laid from the water works to the service reservoir and the provision of 5 per ren:: for contingen- cies. The revised estimates have been approved by the Council who now ask that you will consider them in place of those submitted to the Local Government Board. You will observe that the l total amount necessary for carrying out the proposed work is :£23,150 and not £20,700. The present works (Section 1 of the scheme) consist of 2 boreholes with horizontal engine actuatinte a pump in each borehole, discharging into a covered tank of 200,000 gallons capacity, -te a separate quaeruple acting force pump to deliver a maximum quantity of 24,000 gallons per hour into the district. The aaerage daily supply is about 252,000 gallons, but owing to recent breakdowns arising from mechanical defects in the pumping machinery which are now being remedied, the supply has uot been continuous. The Council have on several occasions been compelled through the want of duplicate machinery to obtain water from the L. S: N.W. Railway Company ; they are therefore most anxious to proceed with the completion of their scheme as quickly as possible. The water has been analysed by Dr. Camp- bell Brown, the Liverpool analyst, and the quality declared to be good. A bacteriological examination has recently been made by Professor Delepine, of Owens College, Manchester, who has pronounced the water to be absolutely safe for drinking purposes. The Council have obtained the advice of Professor Boyd Dawkins, D. Sc.. F. [O., as to the supply of water on the site of the present Water Works. The Professor states that the Triassic eandatones of the district are highly charged with water, and that in his opinion, an ample supply for the needs of the district may be obtained within the area of the present site of the Waterworks. He also approved of the Ccuncirs proposal to sink a well to be I connected with the borings by adits by which means the present yield will be most probably more than doubled and amount to Mere than 500,000

gallons a day. The rateable vahre of the disir.ct is £66,724, and the assessable value £54,962. The rates in the district are as follows : General improvement rate is 2d, highway rate 7d, water rate 3,2 s In the £. The population (last census) was 16,699 and the area of the district is 3,103 acres. The loans outstanding on March 31st 1901 amounted to £28,531 18s 3d. EVIDENCE BY THE ENGINEERS. _

Messrs Read and Waring the engineers, in explaining the present water works said there were two boreholes one 7001 t deep and the other 3001 t. The wat,2r was pumped into a tank and afterwards forced into the mains of the town. When In order the quantity drawn and forced was 24,000 gallons per hour. The popula- tion was 16,699 and the estimated amount required was 300,000 gallons per 24 hours or about 18 gallons per head of population. The aversive amount pumped by the present machinery was 252,000 gallons per day. Mr. C B F Borron, the chairman of the Water Com- mittee. stated that there was sufficient water in the boie holes to meet the supply but they were advised by Professor Boyd Dawkins to open up the rocks and make the supply 500,000 gallons per day. Proceeding with their evidence the engineers said the new proposal was to sink a well between the two existing boreholes to a clepth of 200 feet. Another horizontal engine would be required but they had not gone into the details. The water would be delivered into a high service ;reservoir which it was proposed to erect at Newton Common. A water tower would he plac-d near the reservoir and the contents would be 50,000 gallons. It was proposed to erect one cottage at the pumping statioa and 030 at the reservoir. No provisional agreement had been entered into for the land required. Mr. CB F Borron stated that the land was the sub- ject of negotiation. A price had been named but the figure euggested was net satisfactory to the corn- Fnittee.

The laspector asked to be provided with a plan show- ing the sewerage arrangements of the proposed cottages. (To the Surveyor) : What becomes of the sewerage ? The Surveyor (Hr. Bowes) . It is treated at the Sewerage works. The Inspoctor : What system have you ? The Surveyor ; The bacteriological tank system.
THE MEDICAL OFFICER AND THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

Dr. Watkins, medical cfficer of health for the district, informed the Inspector that there was a necessity for a permanent supply cf water. He eatimated that the population at the present time was 16,308, as compared with 16,699 at the time of the census. Mr. Borron said he would like tie Medical Officer of Health to give the health of the neighbourhood during the time the new supply had been in use. Dr. Watkins stated that the death-rat 3 for the third quarter of the year was 145 per thousand of the population.

The Inspector : I suppose that compares favourably with neighbouring districts ? Dr. Watkins : It is enormously to our advantage. The death rate of our nearest district was 34 per thousand during September last and 28 per thousand for the quarter. As a rule we have a low death rate in the Newton district. . . _
- . The Inspector asked if any rat.payer had any objection to the application. There was no reply.
THE INSPECTOR THANKED. Mr. C. B. F. Borron then proposed a heirty vote of thanks to the Inspector tor the very careful and exbaus- _ _ _

- tive inquiry he had made. He (Mr. Horton) felt sure that'it would give confidence to the inhabitants gener- ally to know that the scheme had had such careful revision. Be also wished to thank the Inspector for his courtesy during the inquiry. Mr. Collingwood seconded the vote of thanks, and stated that the inquiry had satisfied them that their Interests were protected in every possible way. The proposition was cordially carried. The Inrpector, in acknov Ildging the compliment, thanked the Chairman for the kind words he had uttered and said be would endeavour to make a careful report on the matter with as little delay as possible. He recognised that the matter was urgent, in fact, the papers be received from the Local Government Board were marked urgent. The inquiry then closed.

THE CHURCH ARMY. Visit of the Founder to Warrington. There as a very large attendance at the mass meeting fh connection with the Church Army which was held in the Parr Hall on Thursday last week. The announcement that the Rev. W. Carlile, the founder and bon. secretary of the movement, would give an address on the work of the Church Army, aroused con- siderable interest and the hall was well filled. The chair was occupied by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton who was supported on the platform by a number of local clergy.—ln the course of his remarks the Chairman said the work of the Church Army had made itself felt throughout the length and breadth of the country, and he could, to some extent, speak from experience of its work and eommend it to their earnest support. From what he had seen of its work in Warrington he could say it was a very valuable agency and one that should be productive of very great good, not only to church life but to the town generally.— The Rev B Percival, spoke of the good work done by the Church Army in St Peter's Parish.—The Rev W Carlile' then addressed the meeting. He mentioned the fact that the dioceses of Liverpool and Manchester had been in ths forefront in providing fine, earnest young men for evangelistic work. There was yet a tremendous need for workers. The clergy could not do more than they were doing, and it was time for the laity to rise up and feel that there was a priesthood of the laity. The speaker, after dilating upon the good work accomplished by the Church Army, made an earnest appeal for workers, pointing out that the were 100 places vacant at the present moment for earnest men and nearly the same number for earnest women. The work among criminals was mentioned, and the speaker said they must not imagine that be- cause a man had been a long time in gaol he was no good.—A number of Captains and Nurses of the Army gave reminiscences of their work and were listened to with great interest.—An extremely interesting feature of the meeting was the exhibition of a large number of lantern views illustrative of the work of the Church Army in prisons, workhouses, tents, vans, and slums. Mr H. N. Houghton manipulated the lantern—By means of the monsterphone speeches by the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London were distinctly reproduced—A collection was made on behalf of the funds for carrying on the work in Warrington and Liver pool—A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the Rev. W. Carlile on the motion of the Rev. L. J. T. Dar. wall, seconded by Mr. T. E. Gibson, and supported by the Rector, (Rev. Canon Willis). In responding the Rev. , W. Carlile expressed his thanks to the Rev. W. Brace- camp who has acted as secretary in connection with the meeting. The customary montnlv return issued from the War Office states that uring October the British casualties in South Africa, in killed, wounded, etc., amounted to 148 officers and 2.861 men.

LATEST NEWS. Death of Li Hung Chang. PERIN' Thursday, Noon. Li Hung Chang died at eleven o'clock this morning. Li Hung Chang, Genera 1, ex-Prime Minister of China, was born, says "Men and Women of the Time," at Ho Fei Shieun, in the Anu-Huei province, February 16, 1323. He is reported to have been the wealthiest man in the world.
